articles.title: Badenoch claims of Tory air defence plan ‘we haven’t called it Iron Dome’ - despite phrase in press release - UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Conservatives plan ‘new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack

Q: You say your Iron Dome will protect the whole of the UK, and bases abroad. But Sir Richard Barrons,...
articles.body_text:
Conservatives plan ‘new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack

Q: You say your Iron Dome will protect the whole of the UK, and bases abroad. But Sir Richard Barrons, the former general, has said that a proper air defence like this would cost up to £100bn.

Badenoch says Barrons is referring to an Israel-style Iron Dome.

She says she is referring to something different. She says the UK should be able to defend itself from, for example, someone on a boat firing a drone at the system.

Q: But it is nothing like Israel’s Iron Dome. It is a gimmick, isn’t it?

double quotation markIt’s not going to be exactly like the Iron Dome. We haven’t called it an Iron Dome.

But, in fact, they did. This is what they sent out to journalists yesterday.

Q: What would you do in the event of a hung parliament? Would you work with Reform UK?

Badenoch says he does not accept the premise of the question. It is not about uniting the right. It is about uniting the country, she says.

She says even the trade unions agree with her about drilling in the North Sea.

Badenoch says Andy Burnham is not taking tough decisions.

Q: You say he should call an election. But you are polling even lower than you were in 2024. If there is an election now, you won’t be able to turn it round.

Badenoch says people look at who the leader is.

Winning the election is the start, not the end, she says.

She says Labour took office but did not know what it wanted to do. She won’t do that, she says.

She says she has a strong team, a plan, and it’s “all about common sense”.

Q: You are more popular in the polls than your party? Why has that not helped your party?

Badenoch says people still blame the party for what the last government did. She claims people know who is in her shadow cabinet.

Kemi Badenoch is on the Today programme now. Anna Foster is interviewing.

Foster starts by asking about the “Britannia Shield”. Badenoch says that is what they have called it. Foster says in the press released they referred to it as a version of an Iron Dome.

Badenoch says what they are proposing is not like the Israeli version.

Q: £1bn a year won’t get you anywhere close to what you are suggesting here?

Badenoch says they are designing something for the UK.

Badenoch says Foster will have to ask the papers about that. She says the Tories are calling it a Britannia Shield.

Asked about cutting inheritance tax, Badenoch told Times Radio:

double quotation markEven though I want to cut inheritance tax - I’ve given speeches about how I think it is a very bad tax – I’ve been particularly influenced by what we’ve seen over the last couple of years, farmers taking their lives because of them …

But we have to find the money to pay for it. What we’re not doing is just cutting taxes willy nilly. We need to find the savings.

On the missile defence plan, McCann asked Badenoch if this was about protecting the whole of the UK, or just protecting critical infrastructure.

double quotation markI think you are splitting hairs here.

Critical national infrastructure protects the entire country. If we lose even one thing, the entire country is in, is in a real problem.

I don’t want to have a semantic argument. I have put out a description of something which should protect our country and which should make us safer.

Asked if she will propose tax cuts in her speech tomorrow, Badenoch tells McCann that she will have to wait until her speech tomorrow at 11.15am.

(This is getting confusing. On BBC Breakdfast, Badenoch told Jon Kay the speech was at 12pm.)

Q: You say your Iron Dome will protect the whole of the UK, and bases abroad. But Sir Richard Barrons, the former general, has said that a proper air defence like this would cost up to £100bn.

Badenoch says Barrons is referring to an Israel-style Iron Dome.

She says she is referring to something different. She says the UK should be able to defend itself from, for example, someone on a boat firing a drone at the system.

Q: But it is nothing like Israel’s Iron Dome. It is a gimmick, isn’t it?

double quotation markIt’s not going to be exactly like the Iron Dome. We haven’t called it an Iron Dome.

But, in fact, they did. This is what they sent out to journalists yesterday.

Badenoch is on Times Radio now. She is being interviewed by Kate McCann.

Asked when she would raise defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, Badenoch says she has a plan to get to 3%. But she is not in government.

Q: But you say there might be an election soon?

She says she is not in government, and she implies it is unreasonable for McCann to expect her to set out a path to 3.5% when she is not in government.

Q: Would you like to see Penny Mordaunt selected as a Tory candidate?

(At the weekend Mordaunt, the former cabinet minister who lost her seat at the election, revealed she has been approved for the candidates list, which means she can apply to be a candidate in a Tory seat.)

Badenoch says it is not up to her to decide; local parties choose their candidates, she says.

She says she wants “serious people” committed to public service as MPs.

Badenoch says Mordaunt was a “fantastic MP”. She says she was sorry she lost her seat, and is glad she wants to stand again.

But former MPs won’t get special treatment when candidates are being selected, she says. She says she wants candidate selection to be a “meritocracy”.

Q: You are going to cut inheritance tax, aren’t you?

Badenoch says everyone knows she would like to do that. She has said that before.

But she won’t announce that unless she has found the money to pay for it.

Q: Will you have found the money by the time you give your speech tomorrow?

He puts it to her that the UK would need a very different missile defence system from Israel. Israel is under threat from short-range missiles, he says.

Badenoch says it is not just missiles that threaten the UK; drones are a threat too.

Badenoch says it can be done. The £10bn would be spent over 10 years, she says. She says the UK needs to be protected.

They start by asking about the death of Jeffrey Archer, and Badenoch says she got a message from him only yesterday morning. He said: “Great outfit, great speech, no need to reply.”

Badenoch says Archer was “a great communicator” and a “great storyteller”, and someone who believed in Conservatism.

The Liberal Democrats have dismissed the Tory plan for a “Britannia Shield” as “Truss-style fantasy economics”. They say the Conservatives would only get a “Patchwork Dome” with the £10bn they plan to spend on the project.

James MacCleary, the Lib Dem defence spokesperson, said:

double quotation markOnce again the Conservatives are indulging in Truss-style fantasy economics. £10bn would not even touch the sides for a complete UK-wide ‘Iron Dome’. They either need to review their dodgy sums or come clean about which parts of the country their Patchwork Dome wouldn’t cover.

Let’s not forget this is the party that hollowed out our armed forces for a decade, and whose disgraceful plan to fill the defence-spending black hole is based on targeted cuts to the poorest and most vulnerable children. You do not make Britain safer by pushing families into poverty.

This is what the Conservatives are saying about why the UK needs a “Britannia Shield” (their name for what they describe as a version of the “Iron Dome”), and who it would work.

double quotation markThe announcement comes as the threat of missile and drone attack against Britain and our allies continues to grow. Russia bombards Ukraine daily with ever more advanced drones and missiles, and they were behind a drone attack on Leipzig airport in August. Drones launched by Iranian proxies have hit our RAF base in Cyprus, and when Iran fired missiles at the Chagos islands earlier this year, it was the US who stepped in to launch interceptors. Nato allies, especially in the Baltic States, are suffering ever greater numbers of drone incursions and western intelligence agencies have warned that Russia could attack a Nato country by 2030.

We live in an increasingly dangerous and unpredictable world, where threats to the UK and our allies are growing in scale and complexity, yet Britain remains dangerously exposed. A report in November 2025 by the defence select committee warned that, compared to European allies investing heavily in integrated air and missile defence, the UK has “next to nothing”.

The Conservatives will close this dangerous capability gap by committing up to £10 billion over ten years. We will deliver a minimal deployable capability within our first term in office, with the remaining investment focused on expanding and strengthening the system over time.

Britannia Shield will have three key components:

SENSE: New advanced radar systems, to detect incoming missiles and drones.

DECIDE: Upgraded command and control systems to integrate information from across Britain’s defences and rapidly identify the most effective response.

EFFECT: New interceptor missiles, counter-drone capabilities, and significantly larger missile stockpiles to defeat incoming threats.

Good morning. Kemi Badenoch is doing a round of interviews this morning at the Conservative conference, and she will be talking about her plans for the UK to have its own version of Israel’s “Iron Dome” missile defence system. That phrase is not just journalists’ hype; it has come from the first line of the party’s press release, which says the party has plans for a “new integrated air and missile defence system to protect Britain from attack – in essence, a British ‘Iron Dome’.”

Here is our story by Jessica Elgot and Dan Sabbagh.

And this is what Badenoch is saying about it.

double quotation markThe first duty of government is to defend the country and keep people safe. Labour are failing that basic test.

The world will not wait for Britain to get ready. War has returned to Europe. Missiles and drones are transforming warfare in the Middle East. Cheap weapons can now threaten cities, military bases and critical infrastructure in ways that would have sounded like science fiction a generation ago.

If a missile or drone is launched at Britain, we do not get a second chance to wish we had prepared.

The Tories say their plan would cost £1bn a year over 10 years, and that the money would come from the plan they announced last month to raise defence spending by £10bn a year. Almost half the money for this would come from cuts to housing benefit.

7.30am: Kemi Badenoch begins a round of media interviews, starting with BBC Breakfast.

9.45am: The morning session of the Conservative party conference opens, with speeches from Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, then Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary (at 10.30am) and Rebecca Paul, the shadow culture secretary (at noon).

2pm: The afternoon session starts, with speeches from Alex Burghart, the deputy leader, Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign secretary, James Cartlidge, the shadow defence secretary, and Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: NYPD detective released from hospital after being stabbed multiple times in Bronx
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A New York City Police Department detective was released from the hospital after he was stabbed multiple times during ...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A New York City Police Department detective was released from the hospital after he was stabbed multiple times during a robbery in the Bronx last week, according to officials.

Detective Jose Mercedes was wheeled out of Jacobi Medical Center in Morris Park on Monday before standing up in front of a group of clapping officers.

"Today, in another incredible feat of strength and determination, Detective Mercedes got up from his wheelchair and walked out of Jacobi Medical Center on his own two feet. Hundreds of members of the NYPD were there to cheer their brother on," Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said on X.

NYPD DETECTIVE, CHILDREN SHOT IN SEPARATE BROOKLYN SHOOTINGS OVER HOLIDAY WEEKEND

Detective Jose Mercedes was wheeled out of Jacobi Medical Center in Morris Park on Monday before standing up in front of a group of clapping officers. (NYPD)

"The entire department stands behind Detective Mercedes as he continues his recovery. And the greatest detectives in the world will relentlessly pursue those responsible for this crime," she added.

Mercedes was off-duty when two suspects on an e-bike attempted to snatch his gold chain as he was clearing out the trunk of his car in the Norwood neighborhood on Friday afternoon, according to officials.

WATCH: E-BIKE TEEN TAKEOVER SWARMS DOWNTOWN CITY STREETS BLOCKING TRAFFIC, LEADING TO CHARGES

The two attackers remain at large. (NYPD)

The detective attempted to fight back, but he was stabbed and slashed seven times during the struggle before the assailants fled. Authorities said the confrontation began when the men attempted to steal his gold chain.

Mercedes then pursued the fleeing attackers on foot for about two blocks before collapsing near East 206th Street and Rochambeau Avenue.

"Despite his serious injuries, Detective Mercedes chased after his attackers on foot," Tisch said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani visited the detective in the hospital shortly after the attack. (WNYW)

Tisch and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani visited him in the hospital shortly after the attack.

"I visited the detective and his family at Jacobi Hospital with Police Commissioner Tisch," the mayor said on Friday. "I am hoping for his quick and complete recovery."

The two attackers remain at large, police said on Monday.

articles.title: Israeli ambassador to Australia says he hopes for return to ‘traditional friendship’ on October 7 anniversary eve
articles.excerpt:
Relations have soured between the two countries over a number of issues since 2023, but Hillel Newman says a ‘reset’ is possible

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Israel’s ...
articles.body_text:
Relations have soured between the two countries over a number of issues since 2023, but Hillel Newman says a ‘reset’ is possible

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Israel’s ambassador to Australia says the third anniversary of October 7 is an opportunity for both countries to return to “traditional friendship”.

But, in the lead-up to commemorations on Wednesday marking Hamas’ terror attack, leaders of Australia’s Palestinian community say the federal government should do more to help the diaspora suffering since the war on Gaza.

Speaking ahead of the anniversary, Hillel Newman acknowledged relations had become “strained” between Australia and Israel but wanted to see improvement.

“We have challenges, but I have come with a lot of goodwill in order to try and make a positive change in the relationship, perhaps even reset the relationship and return both sides to the initial historical traditional friendship,” the Israeli ambassador told Guardian Australia.

“There have been issues between our two countries. We can have differences of opinion, but we should not allow differences of opinion to overshadow and overcrowd the overall relationship. We can understand if Australia has criticism of this issue or another.”

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The comments come despite Israel’s foreign ministry publicly criticising foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, on social media in recent weeks, branding comments she made to the United Nations about settler violence in the West Bank a “blatant lie”.

It follows an earlier intervention into domestic Australian politics, where Israel urged Labor to soften criticism in a draft policy platform that condemned settler violence and a controversial death penalty law.

Since the 2023 attack – in which Hamas militants killed about 1,200 Israelis and 250 people were taken hostage, in what is considered the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust – there has been a near breakdown in ties between the Israeli government and federal Labor.

Israel’s response to the attack and bombardment of Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians.

Australia has joined other countries in taking an increasingly stronger stance against Israel, including action alongside the UK, Canada and New Zealand to sanction Israeli politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, accusing the two of inciting violence against Palestinians.

But the federal government last month stopped short of joining the UK and other partners in imposing a ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Relations deteriorated further when Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom was killed in a humanitarian convoy struck by Israeli drones in April 2024. Albanese and Wong slammed a decision by the Israel Defense Forces in August not to pursue criminal proceedings over Frankcom’s death.

Pressed on Israel’s failure to release audio from the strike, Newman stressed it was an issue for the Israeli military, but that his country remained open to any request for potential reparations for Frankcom’s family and remained in favour of continued discussions.

Wong has been working with the Frankcom family on an appropriate response to the decision not to press criminal charges.

She said in a statement that the Australian government had condemned the Israeli government’s decision not to pursue criminal proceedings against those responsible for killing Frankcom and her World Central Kitchen colleagues.

“The Australian government will not stop pressing Israel for justice for Zomi and her colleagues. We continue to engage closely with the Frankcom family on further action,” Wong said. 
 “7 October is a day of profound grief and remembrance. We mourn those who were killed in the Hamas terrorist attacks, including Australian Galit Carbone, and all those who have suffered from antisemitic violence around the world.”

The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network president, Nasser Mashni, said the impact from three years’ of war was measured in two places at once: Gaza and in the diaspora.

“In Australia, the impact is a quieter but a relentless erosion of our place in this country,” he said.

“Underpinning every discussion that happens about ‘us’, but without ‘us’, is a nagging suggestion that we don’t belong, that we must prove we are Australian, and even human.

“This is the domestic footprint of genocide: protesting a demand for its end, and stopping Australia’s complicity in it, is more controversial than supporting it.”

In 2025, a UN commission found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, citing tens of thousands of civilian deaths and massive destruction. Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide.

The Greens leader, David Shoebridge, said Australians would reflect on the devastating toll of violence.

“The attacks on October 7 were condemned by the Greens at the time, as our party has a deep belief in peace and non-violence,” he said.

“It is that same core value that means we condemn the ongoing genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.”

The cooler relations between Israel and Australia come against a backdrop of antisemitic attacks in Australia, as the nation prepares to face the first anniversary of the Bondi massacre on 14 December.

Fifteen people were killed by a father-son duo who opened fire on a Hanukkah celebration.

A royal commission sparked by the Bondi attack is due to release its final report on 18 December.

The Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Alex Ryvchin said the October 7 attack and the “unsatisfactory responses” to it meant “troubled, uncertain times lie ahead for us all”.

“But if the jihadists thought mass terror at home and abroad would bring about some global capitulation by Israel and Jewish communities or that the majority of Australians would turn on their Jewish friends and neighbours, they have failed dismally,” he said.

The shadow defence minister, James Paterson, said the October 7 attack had changed Australia in “terrible ways” and culminated in the Bondi attack.

“Fixing this societal cancer will take years of sustained effort from the entire community, from the prime minister down,” he said.

articles.title: Keeping up with the Bolsonaros: Flávio’s surprise first-round election win heralds rise of a political dynasty
articles.excerpt:
Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new president

The we...
articles.body_text:
Four members of disgraced ex-president Jair Bolsonaro’s family have been elected to office, most notably his wife and son Flávio, who won the first round of voting to be Brazil’s new president

The weekend’s elections in Brazil not only put Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the lead in the presidential race, but also underscored how far the former president has come in building a political dynasty.

As his far-right senator son heads into a runoff against the leftist incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a sweeping far-right victory in congressional races also secured seats for Jair Bolsonaro’s wife, two of his sons and one of his brothers.

Few in the family have spent much time working outside politics since the patriarch led the way four decades ago, but the offices they now hold have had a significant upgrade.

Former first lady Michelle Bolsonaro, 44, who divided her campaign with caring for her husband as he serves a sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup, ran for public office for the first time and was elected senator.

Bolsonaro’s second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, 43, regarded as the most radical of the siblings – he ran his father’s social media accounts and was indicted by federal police for leading a so-called hate cabinet that spread fake news and attacks on opponents – was also elected senator for the first time.

His previous political career amounted to 25 years as a city councillor in Rio de Janeiro – starting at the age of 17, when his father put him up for a seat against his own mother, Rogéria Bolsonaro, who had divorced Jair. Carlos won. (Rogéria also ran last Sunday for a seat in the state legislature, still using the Bolsonaro surname, but lost.)

The patriarch’s fourth son, Jair Renan Valle Bolsonaro, 28, who dropped his two middle names on the ballot to run simply as Jair Bolsonaro, jumped from city councillor to federal congressman.

Of Bolsonaro’s five children, only his 15-year-old daughter has never held political office.

Even the former president’s younger brother, Renato Bolsonaro, 62, nicknamed the “brother who can’t win” after losing seven consecutive elections for lower-level offices, was elected. He went from fewer than 10,000 votes in a mayoral race two years ago to 380,000 votes for congress.

During the campaign, Renato caused some friction within the family by saying that “Flávio is not Jair. He doesn’t draw crowds”. At the polls, however, Flávio ended up winning more votes than his father did in 2018 and 2022, although the result is seen by some as more of an anti-Lula vote than a strong preference for the senator.

The number of Bolsonaros in office could have been even higher had “son 03”, Eduardo Bolsonaro, 42, not abandoned his seat in congress and gone into self-imposed exile in the US, where for more than a year he has lobbied for what Lula and many others see as Donald Trump’s attempts to interfere in Brazil’s elections.

Although Michelle is the most recent member of the family to enter politics, it is she who is often considered to be the leading figure among the Bolsonaros. In a July poll, she was named the most powerful woman in Brazilian politics, well ahead of the current first lady, Janja Lula da Silva, in addition to a supreme court justice and many members of congress.

“She is a phenomenon,” said Camila Rocha, a researcher at the Brazilian Center for Analysis and Planning, who has interviewed voters and studied the Brazilian right for a decade. “Even Bolsonaro voters don’t like his sons very much, but many of them like Michelle, who is very charismatic.”

The daughter of a housewife and a retired bus driver from the metropolitan region around Brasília, Michelle was working as a parliamentary secretary for another politician when, at 25, she met Bolsonaro, then a 52-year-old congressman. She is his third wife.

When he took office as president in 2019, Michelle made history by becoming the first and only Brazilian first lady to deliver a speech at an inauguration. She did so in Brazilian Sign Language, which she had mastered while working as an interpreter at evangelical church services – her religiosity is seen as one of the main assets behind Bolsonaro’s close relationship with evangelical voters.

Despite playing by Bolsonaro’s party’s rules, Michelle was at the centre of one of the most contentious moments of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign, when she said that she had been “humiliated”, “disrespected” and “mistreated” by the senator. Reports of friction between her and her stepsons are frequent. Given her popularity, Flávio had to apologise publicly – although Michelle accepted it, the two did not campaign together.

Polls suggested Bolsonaro supporters would have preferred the former first lady as the presidential candidate, but the patriarch opted for his eldest son, and gave her the senate mission instead. “That was the mission my husband entrusted to me, and I will represent him, God willing,” she said in August.

Michelle and Bolsonaro’s sons were also widely seen as helping secure victories for other far-right candidates from Bolsonaro’s party, which will have by far the largest bloc in the next congress.

“Although the family has been in politics for a long time, many voters still see the Bolsonaros as representing ‘renewal’ and an anti-system vote,” said Rocha.

“So, to change everything, these voters want to throw a ‘bomb’ that blows up congress and Lula. And that bomb is the Bolsonaro family,” she added.

articles.title: A medieval manuscript has confounded scholars for centuries. Have they been reading it wrong all this time?
articles.excerpt:
Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text

It has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set ...
articles.body_text:
Researchers argue incorrect binding of Voynich manuscript radically changes ideas about its drawings and indecipherable text

It has been called the world’s most mysterious manuscript: a medieval set of pages filled with botanical drawings, astronomical diagrams, pictures of nude women and indecipherable text. Claimed at various times to be a book in a lost language, a musical score, an instruction manual or just an elaborate hoax, the so-called Voynich manuscript’s true meaning has defied cryptographers and codebreakers for centuries.

Now, new research offers an explanation for why a scholarly consensus over this enduring puzzle has been so hard to come by: not only because its truth is so profoundly mysterious – but because everyone has been reading its pages in the wrong order.

In an article published in peer-reviewed journal Digital Medievalist, Colin Layfield and Lisa Fagin Davis argue that the manuscript’s folded sheets may have originally been piled on top of each other as “singulions” – like a stack of Christmas cards – but were mis-bound in a more typical “nested” arrangement at some point in the mid to late 15th century.

While their finding does not immediately de-code the script, written in what has commonly become known as “Voynichese”, the authors say their finding radically changes our idea of the manuscript’s function.

“There are a lot of people who wanted the Voynich to have been created by one mad genius working in their attic in medieval London or wherever,” said Davis. “In fact, the evidence suggests we’re talking about a more communal object, perhaps a set of booklets through which information was passed down from one generation to the next – the ‘lone genius’ idea is kind of out of the door.”

The manuscript’s unknown provenance has piqued scholarly interest ever since it surfaced in book collectors’ records in the 17th century. When it was bought in 1912 by Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish revolutionary and book dealer with a shop on London’s Soho Square, it was thought to be a scientific diary written by the 13th-century polymath Roger Bacon. Others have credited the codex to Leonardo da Vinci.

Recent chemical analyses of the manuscript, which is held at Yale University, have carbon-dated its parchment to between 1404 and 1438, ruling out these famous authorships.

Some scholars have argued that the text of the Voynich Manuscript is nothing more than gibberish intended as a hoax or a forgery, though recent linguistic analysis has found it more likely that it is written in a natural, if yet unidentified, language.

In 2019, a biology research assistant at the University of Bristol, claimed that the manuscript was written in a “calligraphic proto-Romance” language, but the findings were later disputed, and the university subsequently removed a reference to the claims from its website.

For their article “Singulion Structure and the Voynich Manuscript”, Layfield and Davis used a numerical analysis tool to compare blocks of text and found that many of the attached pages scored highly for coherence even when there were many intervening pages, suggesting the manuscript had been mis-bound.

There were also visual clues suggesting the pages were supposed to be read in a different order. In the current binding, some illustrations of streams or pipes run into the gutter – the blank space along the inner margins where pages are bound – but don’t fully match with the pictures on the opposite page. “Once you treat them as loose pages stacked together, all these artistic anomalies suddenly join up”, said Layfield, a senior lecturer in information systems at the University of Malta.

“Our hypothesis fixes a lot of problems with the structure of the manuscripts in a really elegant way”, said Davis, an expert on medieval handwriting.

She said the only other known medieval manuscripts she has found preserved in a singulion arrangement were Qurans from north Africa, which were likely meant to be handed out as small booklets for instruction purposes.

“I think it’s likely we are looking similarly at an object that was made by a community that wanted to pass its knowledge forward,” said Davis, adding that her hypothesis was supported by paleographical analysis suggesting the manuscript was written by up to five different scribes.

Some of the drawings in the manuscript resemble the female reproductive system, while others hint at herbal lore and astrology. “When you put all of this together, it starts to feel like a book of women’s folk knowledge that’s being preserved,” she said. “But you cannot prove that yet.”

As to the mystery of the manuscript’s language, Davis said it wasn’t out of the question that there would have been other manuscripts written in Voynichese.

“The problem is that so few manuscripts have survived from the middle ages, because they weren’t bound. The irony is that whoever mis-bound this manuscript still did us a huge favour by ensuring its survival.”

articles.title: OpenAI admits response to Australian government hacks 'not good enough'
articles.excerpt:
OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney

OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian gover...
articles.body_text:
OpenAI chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI in Sydney

OpenAI has admitted its actions were "not good enough" after one of its rogue agents breached Australian government websites in June, saying it had added more precautions to its training environments.

The company's chief strategy officer Jason Kwon faced a parliamentary hearing into AI on Tuesday in Sydney, saying the breach "should not have happened" and it "should have handled our response better". It took weeks before Australia was notified via an email to a generic inbox.

"We are sorry and we know we have work to do to rebuild trust with the Australian people," Kwon said.

Anthropic also appeared and said it had not found any cases of Australian breaches during a recent investigation.

Executives from Microsoft and Google were also present.

An OpenAI agent went "rogue" and "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare in June, in what cyber-security experts said was the first hack of its kind.

When asked why OpenAI had not directly contacted government ministers immediately after it found out about the breaches, Kwon acknowledged it was a mistake.

"In retrospect, we should have done what you're suggesting," Kwon said.

"The reason why it happened the way that it did is I think people were thinking about this as a technical situation and they wanted to contact the technical counterparties, but it's not good enough."

Kwon said the company has changed how it handles such incidents.

"Even if we don't fully understand the situation, we are just going to notify and start working through the situation collaboratively with the impacted party."

OpenAI has also added "more precautions" to its training environments since the incidents, Kwon told the 12-member committee, which is made up of Labor, Liberal and independent MPs and senators looking at AI and its impact on Australia.

The company was also establishing a local taskforce in Australia to investigate "how to better manage the risks associated with increasingly capable AI", it said.

Kwon told the committee that training models were now monitored in real time during tests, and that an alarm was triggered if they interacted with the internet in a way they were not meant to.

This meant that OpenAI had been able to alert the New South Wales government to another hack last week within 48 hours.

The company would also support a framework on mandatory disclosure of incidents, Kwon said, as it would set out "clear expectations".

"We were trying to come up with a standard to apply to our voluntary actions… Based on our learned experience here, we should have been probably talking to more people about how to do that well."

Anthropic's head of safeguards Dave Orr said that in the wake of OpenAI agents hacking tech platform Hugging Face in July, it had reviewed "hundreds of millions of transcripts" to detect any potential breaches of Australian government websites similar to OpenAI.

"We haven't found anything like this and we have looked," he told the committee.

The public hearings, which will continue until Friday, also heard evidence from arts and media organisations about copyright and their concerns on how AI models use their materials. AI companies want Australia to relax copyright laws so they can use books and music, for example, to train their AI models.

An opt-out model - where the onus would be on the artist to ask AI not to use their material for training purposes - was flawed and could mean artists do not get paid for their content, the committee heard.

"In other words, Australia's artists will be the roadkill in the rush to this AI deal," said Annabelle Herd, chief executive of the Australian Recording Industry Association.

Anthropic's special envoy Jeff Bleich told the hearing the company had "never tried to dictate" to Australia on its copyright laws.

Why Australia chose the world's biggest political stage to reveal OpenAI hack

What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack

Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?

articles.title: Buckingham Palace says it will not fund Andrew’s legal action against police
articles.excerpt:
Former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest in February

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been warned not to use the king’s private money to fund his legal action a...
articles.body_text:
Former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest in February

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been warned not to use the king’s private money to fund his legal action against Thames Valley police.

The former Duke of York is attempting to quash search warrants that led to his arrest, with a private high court hearing due to take place on Thursday.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend – the amount of which has not been disclosed – provided by King Charles from his private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal defence was a matter for him and his lawyers, and Buckingham Palace had no role in determining its strategy or actions, the source is reported to have said.

The late queen’s second son was arrested on his 66th birthday earlier this year on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after allegations he had shared sensitive information with Jeffrey Epstein during his time as the UK’s trade envoy.

The Telegraph previously reported that Mountbatten-Windsor had been granted permission to challenge whether Thames Valley police acted lawfully over the searches relating to his arrest in February.

A judge at the Old Bailey issued warrants that allowed police to raid his residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge.

On Monday, a judicial spokesperson confirmed a hearing in Mountbatten-Windsor’s legal claim is due to take place at 2pm on Thursday at the high court, before Mr Justice Hilliard.

When Andrew was arrested on 19 February, the king issued a written statement saying “the law must take its course”.

The former duke, who now lives on the king’s private Sandringham estate in Norfolk, was interviewed under caution before being released under investigation.

Police began their searches of the properties on the same day, with the force confirming on 24 February that they had ended.

The judicial spokesperson said the hearing would concern an attempt by Thames Valley police to restrict access to court documents, with the hearing to begin in private.

It is not known whether Andrew will attend the hearing.

A Thames Valley police spokesperson said: “Whilst our investigation into misconduct in public office continues, we are engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the central criminal court.

“As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further.”

articles.title: Will Cristiano Ronaldo play for Portugal after a row with coach Jesus?
articles.excerpt: The drama surrounding Cristiano Ronaldo’s international future took another turn after Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus left the door open for the 41-year-old superstar’s return following his abrupt de...
articles.body_text:
The drama surrounding Cristiano Ronaldo’s international future took another turn after Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus left the door open for the 41-year-old superstar’s return following his abrupt departure from the national team’s training camp.

The sentiment is shared by the Portuguese Football Federation president Pedro ⁠⁠Proenca, who believes the episode is a mere misunderstanding that could be resolved internally.

But how did the apparent rift start, and will Ronaldo ever play again for Portugal?

Ronaldo left the Portugal squad late on Wednesday, shortly after the head coach’s news conference, where Jesus confirmed that the five-time Ballon d’Or winner would be left out of his starting lineup for the match against Denmark, marking a second consecutive Nations League game absence.

Ronaldo’s decision to walk out came as a shock, as he had been due to train with his teammates at the Parken Stadium in Copenhagen.

Portugal’s leading scorer had already spent the entirety of the 2-1 Nations League win away to Norway on September 27 on the bench, having captained the side in the 1-0 home victory over Wales three days before.

The game in Oslo was the first time since November 2024 that Ronaldo had not featured for Portugal despite not being injured or suspended.

Ronaldo appeared to indicate that the reasons behind Jesus’s decision to bench him ran deeper and hinted at a departure from the national team he has graced for more than two decades.

“In due course, I will tell the truth to all the Portuguese people about my reasons for leaving the national team, to which I have always been dedicated,” Ronaldo said in a cryptic Instagram post, announcing his sudden exit from the camp.

Spanish sports daily Marca said Jesus and Proenca followed Ronaldo to Copenhagen airport in an attempt to persuade him to stay with the squad, before the player boarded his private jet.

There were reports that Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro had even discussed the issue of Ronaldo’s involvement with the coach on Wednesday.

Jesus insisted that there was no rift between them, although the 72-year-old, who was appointed in July, acknowledged that his captain was disappointed to remain on the bench against Norway.

Despite his absence, Nations League title holders Portugal won, defeating Denmark 4-2 in Copenhagen and Norway 2-1 in Porto. They also became the first team to qualify for the quarterfinals, ensuring a top-two finish in Group A4.

Forward Goncalo Ramos stepped up in Ronaldo’s absence, scoring three goals to be the team’s joint top scorer along with Joao Felix, while the AC Milan player also bagged an assist.

On Sunday, coach Jesus said Ronaldo could return to the national team ⁠⁠if he chooses ⁠⁠to.

“If he wants to, he’ll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who’s going ‌‌to decide,” said Jesus, who also coached Ronaldo at Saudi Arabian club Al-Nassr.

“He’s the one who should decide how he wants to end his time with the national team. In my first call-up, I said, ‘I need you, I need you to be close to me, playing or not playing, I need you’. And now I’m saying ⁠⁠the same thing.”

Jesus expects the forward to be available for the next international window if he wants to return.

Midfielder Bruno Fernandes said on Saturday he had spoken to Ronaldo and dismissed suggestions of a rift within Portugal’s squad.

“I had a chat with him and what I said to him is ‌‌what I’ll repeat here: the most important thing is that, whatever happens, Cristiano Ronaldo will never cease to be the greatest symbol of our national team, of our football and of the country,” Fernandes told a news conference.

“For what he has achieved not only in Portugal, but all over the world. He has a place reserved not only amongst the all-time greats, but also in the hearts of all Portuguese people.”

“The most important thing is that we ⁠⁠stop stirring up trouble; there are no divisions within the national team. It is ⁠⁠one team and will remain so, despite any noise that may come from outside.”

Fernandes called for unity after a tumultuous few days in which Portugal fans’ opinions have been split over Ronaldo’s decision.

“We are outside of this controversy, but what I ask is that the country does not divide itself, does not make choices, that it respects all sides, but, at the same time, Cris is and will be the biggest icon of our national team. He deserves everyone’s respect, regardless of who likes him more or [who likes him] less,” Fernandes added.

Ronaldo featured just once for Portugal during this year’s Nations League, playing 67 minutes in their 1-0 home win over Wales.

It was a frustrating night for the Al-Nassr forward, who misfired several times. He found the side netting once and shinned an inviting volley high over from close range.

Around the hour mark, Ronaldo slid the ball into the Wales net but, to his evident disbelief, was ruled offside.

He was still shaking his head when Jesus substituted him seven minutes later.

Ronaldo, who made his Portugal debut in 2003 at the age of 18, has said this will “probably” be his final year in football. The forward has been a fixture of the national team for more than two decades and has played at six World Cups.

Former Real Madrid and Manchester United attacker Ronaldo is ⁠⁠Portugal’s record scorer and most-capped player, with 146 goals in 234 international appearances.

He reached the World Cup semifinals in 2006 and captained his country to glory at Euro 2016. Ronaldo and Portugal were eliminated by eventual winners Spain in the last 16 of this year’s World Cup.

Portugal have completed their quota of four Nations League fixtures in this extended international window.

Their upcoming matches are in the next window: a home game with Norway on November 14 and an away match against Wales three days later.

Those matches will wrap up Portugal’s league phase in the Nations League, which they have won twice.

articles.title: From competing for food to a gold medal: the stories behind India’s Asian Games winners
articles.excerpt:
The country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedy

In a country where cricket ecl...
articles.body_text:
The country’s 85-medal haul included athletes who trained with limited money and borrowed equipment. Plus, the Mumbai performer turning everyday absurdities into comedy

In a country where cricket eclipses every other sport, the recently concluded Asian Games offered a much-needed reminder of India’s breadth of sporting talent. In this edition of the games, in Japan, India won 85 medals: 21 golds, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals. I admit I did not know many of the players competing, or even some of the sports they play before putting this piece together. Learning about the stories, I wonder why not.

There were individual breakthroughs, records broken and history made. There were also hard-fought team victories, including the Indian women’s hockey team gold medal after a 44-year wait.

Sports broadcaster Siddharth Pandey cited an old saying in the world of sport: “You cannot be what you cannot see.” For Pandey, one of the most heartening sights was families and communities rallying around the four female players from the north-eastern states. (The region has endured decades of conflict and is often overlooked in the national conversation.) “We simply cannot underestimate the impact these games and medals have on future generations taking up non-cricketing sport and wanting to excel in it,” he told me.

Recognition is also important. Vidya Pillai, the first Indian woman to win a snooker world championship has spoken about her sport not getting the attention or respect it deserves. She felt unacknowledged following her 2023 feat, despite the fact that it came after six unsuccessful world finals and she beat two former world champions along the way.

Behind India’s medal glory are dozens of athletes and families who have struggled financially, trained with limited facilities, and often without much institutional support.

So this week, I am sharing a sample of the many extraordinary stories from different parts of the country. These are only a fraction of the champions to emerge from the games, yet they provide a glimpse of the possibilities that can open up when a country sees and celebrates sporting talent across the spectrum.

Neeru Dhanda (gold in trap shooting): Dhanda’s family in Haryana’s Jind relies on the government’s food subsidy programme and she began her sporting journey using a borrowed shotgun with tin cans as targets. Right before the games began, the 26-year-old spent a few days in a hospital recovering from an illness instead of training. But last week, as rain lashed the shooting range in Urenocho, she became the first Indian woman to win an individual gold in trap shooting at Asian games. She won a second gold in mixed team trap event as well as a silver in the women’s team trap event.

Vithya Ramraj (gold in 4x400m): Ramraj was one of the breakout stars of the event with a three-medal haul. NDTV reported that her father had to borrow money to support Ramraj and her twin sister’s athletic careers. Alongside the team gold in 4x400m, she won a silver in the mixed 4x400m relay. She also broke Indian legend PT Usha’s long-held national record in 400m hurdles which won her a bronze medal.

Sahil Jadhav (gold in compound mixed archery team and men’s compound team): Not long ago, Jadhav contemplated quitting archery, frustrated by not making the progress he had hoped for. He had been forced to compete with borrowed arrows for selection trials, the New Indian Express reported, adding that his mother sold her jewellery to buy him professional compound bows. Now, the 25-year-old has two gold medals and an automatic entry to the 2028 LA Olympics.

Lalremsiami Hmarzote (member of the gold-winning women’s hockey team): The women’s hockey team forward once had to travel about 100 miles from her home to reach the only hockey academy in Mizoram. When she was growing up, her parents had no idea about what hockey and she played barefoot on dirt pitches. This month, playing her 200th international appearance, the 26-year-old struck gold. She scored the lone goal of the final against China, which Hockey India described as a “stunning reverse-stick strike”.

Ancy Sojan (silver in long jump): With colourful beads glistening in her hair, Sojan flung herself 6.53 metres in long jump, to win the silver medal. Earlier this year, the 25-year-old broke the national record set in 2004. Her journey, from a village in Kerala’s Thrissur district to the international stage, has not been straightforward. Last year, she was diagnosed with polycystic ovarian syndrome, forcing her to drastically change her diet and manage the medication-related weight gain she had before the tournament.

Aslam Inamdar (a member of the gold-winning men’s kabaddi team): Inamdar came to kabaddi, a south Asian contact sport combining elements of tag and wrestling, from humble beginnings – he was partly drawn to it because it was affordable and didn’t require expensive equipment. Coming from a village in Maharashtra’s Ahilyanagar, he worked odd jobs – from cleaning washrooms to working in the fields – so he could spend evenings training. “It still feels like a dream to me,” Inamdar told the Indian Express. “I often think about how someone who didn’t even have food at home now holds two international medals.” The 26-year-old was instrumental in helping India win their gold-medal match against Iran.

I would love to hear from you: which sportsperson from the Asian Games did you find most inspiring and why?

Flydubai incident | Indian pilot Smit Machchar is being hailed as a hero for helping to save 174 passengers on the flydubai flight to Israel last week, after his co-pilot made an apparent effort to crash the plane. After being stabbed, Machchar opened the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to enter and overpower the attacker. He is recovering in a hospital in Saudi Arabia, where the plane eventually landed.

Datacentres | Protests against water-guzzling datacentres erupting from the US to Australia are gathering momentum in India. South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen travelled to the small village of Tarluvada, in Andhra Pradesh, where the state government has been accused of fast-tracking plans for a $15bn AI datacentre for Google, allegedly to avoid stringent environmental scrutiny.

Art and design | Designer Vikram Goyal, celebrated for his signature repoussé brass work, brings his installation Wings and Tales to a Georgian townhouse in London’s Mayfair from 12 to 16 October. The exhibition includes furniture designs inspired by landscapes from the Indian epic Ramayana.

A recommendation from someone with great taste

Shireen Gandhy, director of Mumbai’s pioneering Chemould Prescott Road Gallery, founded in 1963, recommends the work of artist Al-Qawi Nanavati. “[She] is a young artist from Bombay whose practice is rooted in printmaking and making her own paper. Her mother’s passing left her with a void,” says Gandhy. Nanavati created Letters to My Mother, an epistolary artwork crafted in, as Gandhy puts it, “a deeply personal language that is not known to anybody but her. Using fabrics and saris that belonged to her mother, she creates this tactile imagery for these letters. I find it very moving and like alchemy.”

This is the number of students from disadvantaged communities who dropped out of some of India’s most prestigious institutions: central universities, Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management between 2018 and 2023, according to Anubhuti Vishnoi of the Economic Times. The figure comes from an interim report by a committee set up by the supreme court last year to examine mental health and suicide prevention in higher education.

Nitesh Shetty’s sketches find absurdity in everyday life, turning familiar characters and social interactions into unexpected punchlines. This is what makes his work powerful: you’re laughing one moment and moved the next. There is a reel for every character imaginable: the person perpetually trapped in the limbo of land disputes, the man who is strangely knowledgeable about funerals, or the friend who has a unique dressing sense.

The 35-year-old from Mumbai didn’t plan on a career in comedy. “When you don’t know what to do, you try anything,” he told me. Now, Shetty rejects more conventional formats such as television in favour of challenging himself creatively. His advice for those who look up to him? “It’s a great time to build something. The [online] audience is ready-made for you. Be original and don’t follow trends.”

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Croatia vs Spain: UEFA Nations League – Yamal, Modric, head-to-head
articles.excerpt:
Who: Croatia vs Spain
What: UEFA Nations League 2026-27, Group A3 match
Where: Stadion Poljud, Split, Croatia
When: Tuesday, October 6, at 8:45pm local time (18:45 GMT)
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport...
articles.body_text:
Who: Croatia vs Spain
What: UEFA Nations League 2026-27, Group A3 match
Where: Stadion Poljud, Split, Croatia
When: Tuesday, October 6, at 8:45pm local time (18:45 GMT)
How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up and live updates from 15:45 GMT.

FIFA World Cup holders Spain can confirm their ticket to the UEFA Nations League quarterfinals when they face Croatia on their trip to Split.

With a perfect record in the tournament and an overall 41-match unbeaten streak, the odds swing heavily in Spain’s favour to clinch victory.

La Roja’s attack has been on fire this term – they have netted 10 goals from seven scorers in three games, with teenage sensation Lamine Yamal leading the scoring charts.

Unlike Spain, Croatia’s performance has been far from exemplary, with Luka Modric’s side suffering their heaviest defeat in history in the last fixture.

Before the clash of generations 2.0 between Yamal and Modric, Al Jazeera breaks down everything you need to know:

The UEFA Nations League was founded in 2018 to reduce the number of meaningless friendlies and give nations competitive matches against equally ranked teams.

In this competition, countries from across Europe participate in a league structure, which features promotion and relegation.

The teams compete across four divisions, facing every other team in their group twice: Once at home and once away. The league phase ends in November.

In the top league, League A, the top two teams from each group advance to the quarterfinals, which take place in March 2027.

The finals will again be contested between four teams. The host and dates of the finals have not been confirmed yet.

Croatia are third in this group with three points from three games.

Spain are first in the group with nine points.

Luka Modric and Ivan Perisic (Croatia): The evergreen Modric, very much the heartbeat of the Croatian midfield even at 41 years old, has found the net once in this campaign. His fellow experienced teammate, Perisic, has also been impactful with his two assists.

Lamine Yamal and Alex Baena (Spain): With four goals in three games, Yamal is the joint leading scorer in this year’s Nations League, alongside three others, including England’s Harry Kane. The Barcelona star has found the net in each game, including a double against Croatia in the initial face-off in Seville. Atletico Madrid’s Baena, on the other hand, has been influential in more ways than one, bagging two assists and a goal.

Centre-back Martin Erlic is sidelined with injury until mid-October, while Josip Juranovic is unavailable due to illness.

Probable Croatia XI: Dominik Livakovic; Josip Stanisic, Luka Vuskovic, Josko Gvardiol, Ivan Perisic; Luka Modric; Franjo Ivanovic, Petar Sucic, Mateo Kovacic, Martin Baturina; Petar Musa

As many as four Spain squad players are doubtful due to injuries: Ferran Torres (physical discomfort), Alejandro Grimaldo (thigh), Joan Garcia (knee) and Nico Williams (thigh).

Probable Spain XI: David Raya; Ivan Fresneda, Robin Le Normand, Aymeric Laporte, Fran Garcia; Rodri, Pedri; Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo, Alex Baena; Roberto Fernandez

You can find your regional broadcaster on UEFA’s official list.

articles.title: ‘Bully in every way’: domestic abuse survivors say ex-partners behind far-right UK street patrols
articles.excerpt:
Seven women share their stories to make people aware of patterns of violence behind anti-immigration street patrol movement

During their relationship, Lisa’s ex-partner was controlling. He kept her a...
articles.body_text:
Seven women share their stories to make people aware of patterns of violence behind anti-immigration street patrol movement

During their relationship, Lisa’s ex-partner was controlling. He kept her at home where he was emotionally and physically abusive towards her, including once attacking her with a machete.

These days, he runs protests outside houses of multiple occupancy that he claims are housing asylum seekers. He coordinates groups of men to patrol the streets of his town, claiming to protect women but often using these patrols to profile and target men of colour.

“There’s nothing good about that man. He’s a bully in every way,” she says.

Lisa is one of seven women who have told the Guardian they are survivors of domestic abuse carried out by key figures in the anti-immigration street patrol movement. All have chosen to come forward to make the public aware of the patterns of violence behind this new form of activism.

At least 14 street patrol groups have been set up in towns and cities across the UK, receiving tens of thousands of pounds in public donations, as well as political support. The deputy leader of Reform UK, Richard Tice, has previously called for more patrols to take place.

Wearing hi-vis jackets and, in some cases, stab-proof vests and carrying handcuffs, these groups of men aim to be a visible presence conducting patrols through their towns and cities. Some have used their patrols to target men of colour, stopping and questioning individuals and demanding to see identity documents.

Despite using rhetoric of protecting women, the Guardian has been shown evidence that indicates the severity of the abuse carried out by men in these groups. Some of the women we have spoken to have been granted restraining or non-molestation orders. One was forced to move towns with the support of the police for her own safety.

“He likes power, and I feel like this is giving him some sort of power. It’s all about power and control in everything he does,” says Lisa, who met and began a relationship with a far-right activist when she was 16.

He is one of the main figures behind the branch of the Raising the Colours movement in his town. The far-right, anti-migrant campaign has hung flags from lamp-posts across the UK under the guise of “patriotism”.

Early in their relationship, Lisa’s partner became abusive and controlling, sometimes preventing her from leaving the house. This behaviour escalated after she became pregnant and had her first child. He would threaten her and her family if she attempted to end the relationship. “I still have nightmares to this day,” Lisa says.

The night that Lisa left him, he tried to attack her with a machete and gave her a black eye and several broken toes. Police attended the scene and arrested him but this was not the end of his abuse, Lisa says. “When I did get away, he was threatening me constantly. I had met somebody else eventually, and I was getting phone calls saying he’s going to kick the baby out of me when he sees me in the street.”

Despite the severity of this abuse, it never resulted in a conviction.

Claire was in a relationship with an anti-immigration activist for several years, during which she made various calls to the police due to his abusive and violent behaviour, which would often be carried out while her children were present.

He was verbally abusive to Claire while she was pregnant, as well as behaving aggressively towards hospital staff after the birth of their first child. This abuse continued after Claire’s pregnancy, including one occasion when he pulled Claire’s hair and gripped her by the throat.

He uses his elevated platform in the town to run street patrols, standing with men outside schools in the mornings and afternoons as children come and go, and erecting St George’s Cross flags on lamp-posts.

The Guardian previously revealed police data indicating patterns of intimate partner violence among 2024 rioters, and similar links can be observed for those involved in these forms of vigilantism.

Last August, Reece McCarron founded the Corby Guard, claiming he had been inspired to set up a group for the Northamptonshire town after seeing someone “making advances to a young girl on the way from school”. On early street patrols he was joined by James Kenna, who had a domestic violence protection order imposed on him in 2020.

A month later, McCarron broke into his former partner’s house, swinging a machete around the kitchen and threatening to kill her. He was later charged with a string of offences including rape, actual bodily harm and intentional strangulation, which have been dropped after support for prosecution was withdrawn by the victim. In May, he was convicted of coercive control, as the prosecutor told the courts “the victim said that she was very scared he would kill her. She couldn’t sleep for weeks.”

In Greater Manchester, Adam Farrell and Jamie Thomason formed the Heywood community guard. Several schools in Heywood were forced to go into lockdown when the guard ran patrols outside their gates.

Farrell was jailed in 2022 after a racist attack on a man that left him with life-changing brain injuries. Thomason has claimed he is “doing God’s work” protecting women and children. In 2018, he was convicted under section 4A of the Public Order Act after arriving at a former partner’s address, banging on her door, threatening to slit her throat and punching her car.

Names have been changed to protect the identity of the survivors of abuse.

articles.title: ‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms
articles.excerpt:
Campaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warnings

In a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met last week t...
articles.body_text:
Campaign groups report surge in membership after a spate of AI safety alerts and apocalyptic warnings

In a bar below Waterloo Bridge, a cell of a fast-growing anti-AI protest movement met last week to plot their latest move: disrupting a tech industry dinner being addressed by a senior executive from the chip maker Nvidia.

Emma, a 28-year-old bartender, had never before taken direct action and was the most nervous of the four plotters from Pull The Plug, one of a growing number of AI-focused campaign groups around the world.

Around the table were a former climate protester and a campaigner versed in the anti-nuclear movement. Emma signed up after a summer of feeling rising alarm at the catastrophic risks of AI, first when a swarm of OpenAI agents escaped their training “sandbox”, cheated, deceived and conspired to hack into the Hugging Face website and then as Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher, quit with an apocalyptic warning that superintelligent AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

As darkness fell they crossed the Thames to the Claremont hotel where Emma filmed while two others unfurled a banner in a function room, shouting “Pull the plug on Nvidia” and “Pull the plug on Palantir”. Hundreds of protesters also staged a rally in front of Palantir’s London HQ last Thursday.

“We did not consent to the kind of build-out that you are planning here,” the activists yelled as they were wrestled out of the door. They edited a video clip – “activist disrupts elite AI network dinner – Nvidia edition” – and uploaded it to Instagram. It was a small gesture, but they had made their stand.

“I want to show other people that they don’t have to feel powerless among all of these articles coming out [about AI doom],” said Emma. “It’s easy to fall into a spiral that it’s too late. This shows people they can address the tech executives, disrupt their meetings, make them feel uncomfortable and get some answers.”

Pull The Plug was launched in January and has about 300 members – mostly aged from 20 to 40. It is backed by an anonymous funder who works in the AI industry, organisers said. Several campaigns resisting AI acceleration are funded by tech insiders.

Pull The Plug advocates direct action – a tactic other AI campaigns have rejected. Last month, one of its members climbed on to a chair in a packed AI conference in London addressed by speakers from OpenAI and Amazon and delivered an impassioned speech.

“Best case scenario: the men handling this technology are completely incompetent,” the female activist said in an outburst that garnered 153,000 Instagram likes and was picked up by the Washington Post. “Worst case scenario: we are all being led into a disaster.”

Other AI protest movements are gaining momentum after a torrent of news about AI dangers. Anthropic told investors this week that advanced AI could pose “existential risks to humanity”. Pause AI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries, saw a fourfold jump in sign-ups when worrying news about rogue AI agents was breaking in August and last month.

“We have had a lot of volunteers who have suddenly decided to dedicate way more of their time to the cause,” said Maxime Fournes, a Cambridge-educated mathematician and deep learning engineer who is chief executive of PauseAI Global. Volunteer sign-ups doubled to about 100 a week after the Hugging Face incident and soared to 681 in the week of Coxon’s “kill us all” warning, when PauseAI organised protests in Paris, London and Berlin.

Donald Trump may be one of the movement’s most important recruiting sergeants. He announced last week that he wanted AI companies to “self-police” despite widespread demands, including from the companies, for federal and international rules to limit AI-enabled cyber-attacks and bioweapons.

The surge in worrying news has given campaigners like Fournes hope that “we could actually survive this situation”. He added: “Suddenly we have a large fraction of the world population that is waking up.”

Joseph Miller, an AI safety researcher who has suspended his doctoral studies at Oxford University to run Pause AI’s UK branch, noticed the shift while campaigning outside Brixton tube station in London. He said: “It was the easiest flyering we’ve ever done, because people would just come and talk to me … one every few minutes.”

People he spoke to were worried about cognitive decline in schools and AI resulting in sloppy work in the office. “I heard ‘killing everyone’ more from young people,” Miller added.

Pausing or halting AI is a cause that cuts across political and generational boundaries, according to campaigners. University students sign up because they fear AI will wreck career paths, while older conservationists rally against datacentre construction.

In Scotland, where at least 21 datacentres are planned, Action to Protect Rural Scotland, a 100-year old charity better known for campaigning for green belt land, said its supporter list had swollen from 400 to 4,000.

“I’ve never seen grassroots energy like this,” said Kat Jones, the charity’s director. She affectionately calls it “a campaign of nerds” with supporters probing the workings of AI datacentre cooling systems and the power grid and lodging freedom of information requests.

AI’s need for vast physical infrastructure has provided a “very physical, concrete object of protest”, said Fournes, and, in some cases, a target for direct action. In the last year, far-left or anarchist groups protesting over the climate crisis and AI have claimed responsibility for criminal attacks on infrastructure in France and Germany.

In August, Wynd Kaufmyn, became the first anti-AI protester believed to have been jailed for taking direct action – in her case blocking the entrance to OpenAI’s HQ in San Francisco. In April, another protester hurled a petrol bomb at the house of the company’s chief executive, Sam Altman. The same month, an attacker fired gunshots into the home of an Indianapolis politician in protest at datacentre plans.

Mauro Lubrano, assistant professor of terrorism and political violence at the University of Leiden, said that if rising demands for accountability, transparency, and democracy in AI governance were not met, more people could get drawn to violence.

“It’s quite likely that we will see anti-AI violence becoming more prominent as a driver to political violence,” he said, citing last month’s vandalism of a Canadian AI institute, Mila, and a nearby software company in Montreal. Windows were smashed and graffiti scrawled reading “burn the data centers”.

Some Pull The Plug activists have diverted their energy from Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion. One member of Emma’s cell glued herself to roads to protest against the climate crisis – tactics that have alienated the public.

Such direct action is “extremely counterproductive”, said Fournes who predicted it would trigger “an immune response” from wider society and would provide “a golden opportunity for the AI labs … to say, they are criminals and it is easier to turn the broader public against the movement against the development of AI”.

Whatever the tactics, a movement is stirring.

articles.title: Australian consumer confidence plunges to worst level since 1990s after RBA rate rise
articles.excerpt:
Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households ar...
articles.body_text:
Key indicator dropped about 20% after the Reserve Bank last month announced the highest interest rates since 2011

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households are the most persistently pessimistic they have been since the early-1990s recession, after a fourth rate rise this year.

Confidence among Australian consumers has plunged about 20% since the Reserve Bank of Australia lifted interest rates to the highest levels since 2011, according to the Westpac–Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index.

The survey, conducted between 28 September and 1 October, showed the confidence index dropped by 4.7% to 80.4% in October – the worst level since the outbreak of the Middle East conflict in early April.

But for respondents surveyed after the RBA call on 29 September, the index dropped to 67.2% – the lowest level since the late 1990s.

That was broadly in line with the weekly ANZ-Roy Morgan consumer survey, which fell about 5% to 67.1 points.

Westpac’s head of Australian macro-forecasting, Matthew Hassan, said sentiment had been extremely weak for the longest period since the “disastrous” recession of the early 1990s.

“Australian consumers remain stuck in a cost-of-living nightmare that seems to have no end in sight,” Hassan said.

“The latest RBA move looks to have badly rattled consumers. Responses over the course of the survey week show a very sharp deterioration after the decision was announced.”

Assessments of family finances and buyer sentiment were the biggest categories affected.

Expectations about the economic outlook fell less sharply, but assessments about the economy in the next five years were back to lows not seen since August 2020, shortly after Melbourne’s second lockdown and before jobkeeper subsidies were expanded.

AMP economist My Bui said the decline was unsurprising given the September rate hike and rising fuel prices.

“On our calculation the weekly petrol bill for a typical Australian household has gone up by $20 versus the beginning of the year,” Bui said.

“The worry with declining confidence is that it tends to correlate with household spending on a per capita basis: the downtrend in confidence over the past 12 months suggests consumption per person will likely fall further into contraction this year.”

Mortgage holders were the most pessimistic home ownership subgroup given rising borrowing costs at 77 index points.

Those who own their home outright experienced the largest decline in sentiment in the month, as the housing market downturn extended for a sixth month.

Renters were the most optimistic, unchanged at 84.8 points.

Hassan said fears of job losses were rising, with unemployment expectations ticking up 1.9% higher. But there are still signs the labour market is holding strong.

Citi analysts Josh Williamson and Faraz Syed said “job vacancies have increased to a two-year high of 122 points, which accords with business sentiment expectations of positive employment growth”.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Why the Green party’s Zionism vote has caused a backlash
articles.excerpt: In today’s newsletter: The party has voted to define Zionism as racist and back a single Palestinian state. But what does the policy mean, why has it caused alarm among Jewish members, and how will it...
articles.body_text:
In today’s newsletter: The party has voted to define Zionism as racist and back a single Palestinian state. But what does the policy mean, why has it caused alarm among Jewish members, and how will it impact the future of the Greens?

The Green party of England and Wales is in turmoil. Following a vote to adopt a policy that equates Zionism with racism, and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”, some Jewish members say they are considering whether they are welcome in the party.

While Green members celebrated, or mourned, the motion passing, some have questioned its purpose, arguing it will distract from what’s important – keeping eyes on Gaza and holding the Israeli government to account – instead igniting a divisive discussion about ideology that will only harm the party.

Today, I spoke to Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland, to understand how the vote has been received by many Jewish people beyond the Greens, and senior political correspondent Peter Walker, who reported on the fallout of the vote at the party conference in Brighton at the weekend. That’s after the headlines …

RAF Fairford | No 10 has insisted the Gloucestershire base is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers that had been stationed there amid security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.

Donald Trump | Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%.

Brazilian elections | Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former president Jair Bolsonaro, is poised to win the Brazilian presidency, after a shock first-round victory.

Jeffrey Archer | Jeffrey Archer, the bestselling author and former MP whose political career ended in disgrace when he was imprisoned for perjury, has died at the age of 86.

Cancer | Cases of seven types of cancer have risen sharply among younger people in England, major new research has found, prompting warnings that lifestyle choices are costing thousands of lives each year.

Yesterday, the head of the Jewish Greens Vivien Lichtenstein confirmed that she is considering leaving the party after Sunday’s vote. Many other Jewish Greens – a significant majority of whom described themselves as anti-Zionists when polled – are similarly taking stock.

Much of the fallout was predictable. The chief rabbi, Ephraim Mirvis, described the motion as “poisonous antisemitism” and Israel immediately barred Zack Polanski, the Green party’s Jewish leader, from entering the country. The Israeli foreign ministry denounced the motion as “a stain on the history of the United Kingdom”.

With four of the Green’s five MPs opposing the new policy, yesterday evening the group representing European Green parties expressed dismay at the move which runs counter to their support for a two-state solution for Israel and Palestine. There is now growing anger internally with Polanski, who avoided the debate to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where he is running for former prime minister Keir Starmer’s seat.

What is the motion about – and who supports it?

Zionism isn’t a clearly defined, singular ideology. Broadly speaking, it means support for Jewish self-determination, realised today in the state of Israel. The motion argues that Zionism is racist because it “privileges one ethnic group on the basis of the subjugation of others” and that in Israel this is based upon “European settler-colonial systems of domination and oppression”. It adds: “This motion is aimed at the political ideology and practice of Zionism … and not at the religious or ethnic background of those who may identify as Zionists”.

Prior to this, senior Greens have been some of the most vehement voices in the UK in condemning Israel’s destruction of Gaza, which a UN commission of inquiry found to be a genocide. They have also spoken out against the ongoing occupation of the West Bank, as well as pushing for a full arms and trade embargo.
