articles.title: Anticipation builds as MIke Tomlin prepares to unveil his Minecraft city that's 12 years in the making
articles.excerpt: Cal and Jody hear from a caller wanting to talk about the Chicago Bears. That’s as normal as sports radio gets, until it starts to seem like this listener could be phoning in from across time and spac...
articles.body_text:
Cal and Jody hear from a caller wanting to talk about the Chicago Bears. That’s as normal as sports radio gets, until it starts to seem like this listener could be phoning in from across time and space.

The 2026 NFL season is the first without Mike Tomlin somewhere on the sidelines in decades.

And while the former Steelers coach has moved into the world of TV broadcasting, he's about to become a big deal in a corner of the internet no one would've expected a few months ago.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Mike Tomlin is preparing to give fans a look at his much-talked-about Minecraft city. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images)

That's right, the longtime Steelers head coach is about to let fans into the blockified city he has been crafting for the last twelve years.

"It was therapeutic for me," Tomlin said in a video posted to social media. "It allowed me to detach from the pressures and the reality of life. Kind of my secret obsession, and so let's take you all through it."

The video then teased the release of a full video on Tomlin's YouTube channel, which showed an aerial view of a city that had a baseball field, streets, and even buildings with what looked to my eye to be HVAC equipment on the roof.

BREAKING UP TROY AIKMAN AND JOE BUCK WOULD BE A BIG MISTAKE FOR ESPN | BOBBY BURACK

The "NBC Sunday Night Football" analyst revealed in an interview around the start of the season that he was a big fan of the building game that has become a cultural phenomenon over the years.

RAMS COACH SEAN MCVAY'S '60 MINUTES' INTERVIEW REVEALS WHY YOU SHOULDN'T FIND YOUR IDENTITY IN YOUR JOB

Being an NFL coach is such a high-pressure job with a lot of noise. How better to get a break from that than by focusing all of your attention on the 8-bit stadium you're trying to construct?

Minecraft has become a cultural phenomenon, and Mike Tomlin is all in on it. (Photo by Alexander Bogatyrev/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

I can't think of one, and it's a pretty healthy way to tune everything out and get yourself focused on the present.

If you're wondering how he was able to handle being an NFL coach for so long, well, for twelve of those years, this is your answer.

Now that Tomlin isn't leading an NFL team anymore, he's got more time to devote to Tomlinburg (or whatever he calls it), and I expect it to be looking like Tokyo in a few months.

articles.title: California superintendent candidate calls out teachers union, says she's a 'real threat' to 'socialist agenda'
articles.excerpt: Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California state superintendent of public instruction, rocked a California Interscholastic Federation meeting to deliver a boisterous argument advocating for the protection...
articles.body_text:
Sonja Shaw, a candidate for California state superintendent of public instruction, rocked a California Interscholastic Federation meeting to deliver a boisterous argument advocating for the protection of girls sports (Credit: Sonja Shaw).

Conservative California superintendent candidate Sonja Shaw told Fox News Digital Tuesday she would not back down from confronting the United Teachers Los Angeles union (UTLA) after a circulated video allegedly showed a union leader calling Shaw a "real threat" and warning that her election "would cause a huge problem for us."

Shaw, the president of the Chino Valley Unified School District board, pointed to Los Angeles student achievement scores as she accused UTLA of protecting the education establishment rather than focusing on academic outcomes.

"I’m not surprised the Los Angeles teachers union sees me as a threat," Shaw said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"More than half of their students still can’t read at grade level, and nearly two-thirds can’t do math. Instead of working to help those kids, UTLA has fought to keep parents in the dark, excused failure and protected the system that produced these results."

NATION’S LARGEST TEACHERS UNION UNDER FIRE AS CONTROVERSIAL AGENDA PUTS CENTURY-OLD FEDERAL CHARTER AT RISK

Sonja Shaw said the recording showed union opposition to her campaign. (San Francisco Chronicle via Getty)

California’s latest official assessment results lend context to Shaw’s criticism of Los Angeles Unified’s academic performance.

In 2025, 46.46% of LAUSD students met or exceeded the state standard in English language arts and 36.76% met or exceeded the standard in mathematics, according to California Department of Education testing data. That meant roughly 53.5% did not meet the ELA standard and 63.2% did not meet the math standard.

Shaw said the criticism described in the video would not change her approach to the statewide race.

"If putting children and families first is a ‘huge problem’ for their agenda, that tells you everything you need to know. I won’t back down," she said. "They just admitted it. I’m a ‘real threat’ to their socialist agenda. Parents over politics. Kids over ideology. Girls over boys in their sports and locker rooms. Keep calling me a threat. I’ll keep being one."

WATCHDOG REPORT EXPOSES TEACHERS UNION 'POLITICAL MACHINE' FUNNELING MORE THAN $1 BILLION TO LIBERAL CAUSES

DeAngelis, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation who posted the recording on X, told Fox News Digital he viewed the purported remarks as evidence of organized labor’s opposition to Shaw. (Getty Images)

In the clip, shared by Corey DeAngelis, a research fellow at The Heritage Foundation, a woman describes Shaw as a "real threat" and discusses efforts to prevent a "MAGA lady" from taking charge of public education.

The woman then warned about what Shaw taking office would mean for the organization.

"That would cause a huge problem for us," the woman said.

The California Post reported the speaker was Julie Van Winkle, the UTLA AFT vice president.

HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES PROBE INTO 5 MAJOR LABOR UNIONS OVER DEM SPENDING DESPITE MAGA MEMBERSHIP BASE

UTLA had endorsed Shaw opponent Richard Barrera, and organized labor spent millions backing him in the statewide race. (AndreyPopov/iStock/Getty Images Plus)

DeAngelis told Fox News Digital he viewed the purported criticism as evidence that Shaw was threatening teachers unions’ political influence.

"This leaked audio is the best endorsement Sonja Shaw could’ve ever received. When a power-hungry teachers union that fights to protect itself at the expense of kids calls you an existential threat to their socialist agenda, you’re officially over the target," he said.

UTLA has publicly endorsed Shaw’s opponent, San Diego Unified School District Board President Richard Barrera, for California superintendent of public instruction. The union says Barrera has a "proven commitment" to working with educators and families and called for a superintendent who would work with unions on education funding.

Organized labor has also spent millions supporting Barrera.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

California Secretary of State data compiled by CalMatters showed the California Teachers Association Independent Expenditure Committee had spent $5,057,539 supporting Barrera as of Sept. 15, compared with $10,000 in reported outside spending supporting Shaw.

Los Angeles County Republican Party Chair Roxanne Hoge also pointed Fox News Digital to a post from Saturday on X tying the controversy to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s recent overhaul of the superintendent’s authority.

"We knew [Sonja Shaw] was causing good trouble when [Gavin Newsom] stripped the office she's running for of most of its power," she said.

Fox News Digital reached out to UTLA and Newsom's office for comment.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

articles.title: The children dying in India's remote tribal heartland
articles.excerpt:
Koushila Markam holds a photograph of her daughter, Bamita, who died aged three

Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing

At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Marka...
articles.body_text:
Koushila Markam holds a photograph of her daughter, Bamita, who died aged three

Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing

At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing.

The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment.

Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead.

"She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday.

Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups", external.

Atilal Dhurwey holds a framed photograph of his 17-year-old brother Rooplal, who died in June. Rooplal died days after developing a fever and rash.

Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria,  possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment.

They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain.

"I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me.

But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself.

In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain.

The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain.

Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died.

Behru Markam lives with his wife and four children in a mud hut. His daughter, Preeti, died of a suspected measles attack.

The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages.

When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her.

"If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says.

Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived.

For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death.

The Dhurwey family home in Bondari village is nearly 2km uphill from the nearest road

For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge.

On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area.

"Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished."

When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly.

"Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered."

Mahasingh Parte, who lives in Matla village, lost two children within two days of each other

In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered.

By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri.

The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic, external, fever could mean several things at once.

Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the children to a doctor.

Her husband, Samaroo Dhurwey, remembers nights in which the children's bodies seemed to be "on fire". They could not digest food. They died at home.

Mahasingh Parte of Matla village lost two children - a six-year-old girl and a four-year-old boy - within two days of each other. The family followed a faith healer's instructions. "He said don't take them to hospital," Parte recalls.

Koushila Markam visits the grave of her three-year-old daughter, Bamita, marked by a pile of large rocks beside a paddy field

Parte is a landless farm labourer who earns about 200 rupees ($2; £1.58) on a good day, he said. Work is scarce in the monsoon, and although a small primary health centre is just 5km away, he had never been there. Poverty and remoteness had stacked the odds against his children.

The question of what was making children sick became harder to answer as the deaths mounted.

An investigation by the ICMR-National Institute for Tribal Health Research (NIRTH) tested 10 samples collected from the affected villages on 7 August. Six tested positive for measles; four were negative.

Measles is highly contagious, causing high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash. Most children recover, but malnutrition can make measles far more dangerous, external, increasing the risk of pneumonia, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, and inflammation of the brain. The infection also weakens the immune system, leaving children vulnerable to other infections. Malaria can compound that risk.

But doctors cautioned that malaria did not necessarily follow measles, and not every fever and rash was measles. Instead, several infections and vulnerabilities collided.

Sick children were brought to a health camp in Kondekasa village during the outbreak

"Sometimes there is no single factor behind the deaths," Gautam said. "There are malnourished children and there's zero health education and hygiene at home."

The Baiga villages are not entirely disconnected from modern India. Seasonal migration takes families to other states for chilli picking and other work. Children watch reels on smartphones, while many families have minimum single-bulb solar-powered electricity, bank accounts and, in some homes, piped water.

Yet malnutrition remains widespread, with children often poorly fed. A five-year-old who died recently of measles weighed around 5kg.

Gautam believes malnutrition is driven by early marriage and motherhood, with some girls becoming mothers at 16 or 17, when their bodies are still developing.

Closely spaced pregnancies, premature births and low birth weight can follow, while young mothers struggle to breastfeed and care for their children. Diet is another problem: many families rely heavily on rice and lentil soup, with too little protein and dietary variety. Studies on Baiga households have found widespread nutritional deficiencies, compounded by poor uptake, external of public services.

The gap between services on paper and on the ground was stark: the state response came weeks after deaths began, while health teams struggled to reach and persuade families.

Malnutrition remains widespread among children in Balaghat's Baiga community

Once the outbreak was recognised, health workers began door-to-door screening in affected villages. Mobile medical units carrying oxygen, nebulisers, suction equipment, malaria tests and medicines visited more than 20 affected villages.

One mobile doctor, Neeraj Sharma, says teams routinely saw more than 50 patients a day, about half of them children. They conducted 10 or more malaria tests daily, sometimes finding two positive cases a day.

More than 6,200 patients - mostly children - were eventually treated at home, according to Gautam. More than 630 were referred to district hospitals. About 600 returned home, while around 30 remain admitted.

Vaccination became an emergency response. Although official records suggested 90-95% coverage in some areas, health workers found children without records and families reluctant to vaccinate.

Authorities therefore offered the measles-rubella (MR) vaccine to all children under 15, regardless of recorded status. Of about 40,000 children identified in Birsa, roughly 27,000 had been vaccinated, Gautam said. Of the area's 180 villages, some 67 are predominantly Baiga and among the most vulnerable.

But vaccination is only one part of the protection children need. There are wider questions about whether basic nutrition and other health services are reaching those most at risk.

A 2024 audit by India's Comptroller and Auditor General found "serious irregularities", external in Madhya Pradesh's distribution of take-home rations meant to supplement the diets of children aged six months to three years, pregnant women and lactating mothers, including problems with beneficiary identification, production, transport and distribution.

The outbreak has now subsided. Officials say the last child death was more than two weeks before their late-September assessment, while teams continue visiting villages. In Kundekasa, a medical camp that once saw about 120 children a day was seeing fewer than 10.

Back in Matla, Bamita's mother speaks about the child who would ask for money for snacks, play with her sister and run inside whenever cars approached because vehicles frightened her.

"I had hope she'd study and make something of herself. I never regretted I didn't have a boy," Koushila says.

Then she looks at Ankita, the surviving sister.

"I want more kids," she says. "I feel alone. Ankita is alone. She keeps crying for her sister."

articles.title: ‘We beat Disney, Fauci, Soros’: Ron DeSantis unleashes ‘Florida model’ in hard-hitting midterm rally
articles.excerpt:
Rejecting poll-driven politics, Gov. Ron DeSantis makes the case for congressional candidate Dan Green by detailing his administration’s battles with Disney, unions and federal mandates.

Pitching his...
articles.body_text:
Rejecting poll-driven politics, Gov. Ron DeSantis makes the case for congressional candidate Dan Green by detailing his administration’s battles with Disney, unions and federal mandates.

Pitching his administration’s conservative record as a national blueprint for Capitol Hill, Gov. Ron DeSantis rallied Republicans in Osceola County Tuesday night, portraying Navy veteran Dan Green’s bid for Florida’s 9th Congressional District as part of a broader push to bring aggressive Florida-style governance to Washington.

Speaking before a crowd in St. Cloud, south of Orlando, DeSantis pointed to his administration's high-profile battles on education policy, state spending reductions and corporate pushback and urged voters to bring that same combative, policy-driven mandate to the halls of Congress.

SOCIAL MEDIA ERUPTS AFTER DESANTIS GIVES ‘SOROS’ PROTESTER A PIECE OF HIS MIND: ‘AIN’T MY FIRST RODEO’

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaks at the Republican National Convention at the Fiserv Forum July 16, 2024, in Milwaukee, Wis. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

"I will say that I'm looking forward to y'all getting the congressman elected that has served this country and that has served for the right reasons. Now, I am a big believer that we need term limits for members of Congress. But until we do that, you can show your current guy the term limit by kicking him out of office.

"So, I think what we need is what we've done in Florida. It can be a model for people like Dan going to Washington, other states, you name it, because it's not just about peacocking and putting social media press releases out and never getting anything done. We have fought every big fight that there has been to fight in the state of Florida, and we have won every big fight that there is to fight in Florida."

DeSantis rallied the conservative faithful with a recap, alleging major victories over left-wing institutions, agencies and agendas.

"Just think about it. We beat Dr. Fauci on COVID. We beat Disney on gender ideology. We beat Soros on crime by removing two of his prosecutors. We beat Martha's Vineyard on illegal immigration.

"We just beat the Muslim Brotherhood by banning Sharia law. We beat the teachers unions by enacting universal school choice for all Florida families. We beat SEIU by doing paycheck protection.

Republican Florida Gov. Ron Desantis  (Fox News)

"Every single time there was a fight, we would beat and win the fights. And that's ultimately what it's all about. Because leadership — when it's popular, when it's easy — anyone can do that. 'I'll just go with the flow,' all this other stuff. It really matters when it is tough and when you're going to face arrows."

TRUMP'S HANDPICKED DESANTIS SUCCESSOR WINS CROWDED GOP PRIMARY FOR FLORIDA GOVERNOR

DeSantis repeatedly emphasized that his top priority was sticking to the courage of his convictions, not seeking political expediency or going along to get along.

"I remember during COVID, I was doing things, and people said, 'Oh, he's not shutting down the beaches. Why does he have these people in school?' And all this other stuff. You know, people come after you, and a lot of people told me that I was frittering away my governorship, that I wouldn't be able to win in '22, and all this other stuff. I don't know if that was true. Who knows, right?

"But when you get in a position to lead, you either do it or you should just sit down. My job was not to be worried about my own political hide. My job was to be worried about protecting the liberty, jobs, and businesses of the people I was elected to serve. So, we started the fire, and we gave them his right."

It is clear that the two-term governor considers his famed battle with Disney to be a particular feather in his cap.

"Nobody in the history of the state had ever taken on Disney in anything. A lot of people told me I was making a mistake," DeSantis said.

"But the reality is, do we want a society in which our 6-year-olds are being told they can change genders, or do we want a society rooted in truth? If you want a society rooted in truth, even if the biggest, most powerful corporation in the state is against you, you've got to stand up and you've got to fight. And we fought, and we won."

As the federal debt has topped a staggering $40 trillion, DeSantis made the case that he has taken the state on a markedly divergent course.

"Just look at the results. For four straight years, Florida has reduced its budget. Is any other state in the country reducing spending? We've done it four years in a row," DeSantis said.

"I was just able to announce today if you take all of Florida's debt for all of our history up until the time I became governor, just in my tenure, we will retire 54% of the state's debt, more than cutting it in half.

"We've been ranked No. 1 for education freedom, and our public university system is ranked No. 1. We have the lowest in-state tuition of any state in the United States, and it's the exact same cost today to students and families that it was the day I took office.

"It did not go up one penny under my tenure. Is there anything else that didn't go up? The dollar menu at McDonald's is all $2.99 now. Everything else has gone up, but that has not gone up."

Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, Dr. Anthony Fauci and President Donald Trump. (Getty/AP)

And DeSantis touts Florida as a national leader in lowering taxes for its citizens and called for voters to back Amendment 3 in Florida, which would pave the way for elimination of non-school property taxes.

"If you look at tax relief, we've done $10 billion over my tenure — more than anyone. Some of it is permanent, like no tax on baby items, back-to-school items and no tax on business rent. But, really, the big enchilada is going to be on the ballot in November when you have a chance on Amendment 3 to vote yourself more control over your own home and not let them tax you to death. So vote yes on 3.

As Republicans face headwinds heading into the midterms in a little over a month, DeSantis drew a parallel between this year's election, and the 2018 election, which propelled him to the governor's mansion by a narrow margin.

"We've done all this stuff, but I think the lesson is this: When I won eight years ago, it was kind of similar to how it is now. People were saying it was a ‘blue year.’ There was a lot of wind in the face of Republican candidates," DeSantis recalled.

"A lot of people thought Florida was a swing state — that we were purple — where one point had decided all these races for the previous decade. A lot of people didn't think I could even win given those circumstances. And even if I won, they said, 'Well, the state's going to go blue. You've got all these people moving from Puerto Rico, the Northeast, anything.' So, I'm running. It wasn't easy, and we won."

DeSantis maintains he has never taken a poll as a means to determine a position on an issue.

"It was a close race, so I had a choice to make: Do I try to tiptoe around the tulips, not offend anybody, and just try to walk this tight line? Or do I say, 'You know what? I won the election. I got 100% of the executive power, and I didn't get elected to follow. I got elected to lead,'" DeSantis said.

"So, I am going to fly the banner of bold colors, not pale pastels. I'm going to do what I believe in. I am not going to take any polls. I have not to this day ever polled a single issue in my entire time as governor.

"The reason is simple. … It depends on how you ask the question, right? I can tweak the words and get a different result. But also, what does a poll actually mean? Like Popeye said, ‘I am what I am,’ right?"

David Unsworth reports on Latin America. You can follow David Unsworth on Twitter @LatinAmerUpdate

articles.title: Pennsylvania confirms fifth measles-associated death as US outbreak grows
articles.excerpt:
Pennsylvania has confirmed a fifth measles-associated death this year, as the number of infections approaches 1,000 amid a rapidly growing outbreak across the state.

The Pennsylvania Department of He...
articles.body_text:
Pennsylvania has confirmed a fifth measles-associated death this year, as the number of infections approaches 1,000 amid a rapidly growing outbreak across the state.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health announced on Wednesday that an unvaccinated resident of Lancaster County who tested positive for measles had died.

The department said the death was reported to the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The state has recorded 943 confirmed measles cases across 39 counties so far in 2026, including 40 new cases since September 28. At least 176 people have been hospitalised.

The US is currently seeing the worst measles outbreak in the country since 1991, with several deaths reported over the last couple of years.

Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, but the highly infectious disease has made a comeback in recent years, a trend some experts have linked to a rise in vaccine scepticism.

The latest death is the third associated with measles reported in Lancaster County this year.

Located in the south-central part of the state, Lancaster County is considered the centre of Pennsylvania Dutch Country, home to the nation’s oldest Amish and Mennonite communities. Both communities have under-vaccinated populations.

Pennsylvania announced its first two measles-associated deaths in August, the first measles-related deaths recorded in the state in 35 years. Since then, the number of confirmed infections has more than doubled.

The growing outbreak has prompted the administration of Governor Josh Shapiro to expand vaccination efforts and public health outreach.

Protection is most commonly conferred through a combination injection known as the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, or the MMR shot.

According to Pennsylvania’s Department of Health, more than 53,000 MMR vaccine doses were administered statewide in September, more than twice the number given during a typical month. Health experts say that two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles.

On Tuesday, the CDC confirmed two measles-related deaths in its national tally, though the agency did not identify where the deaths occurred.

The federal count has been at the centre of a dispute between Shapiro and US Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr over how measles deaths are classified.

Pennsylvania has reported five “measles-associated” deaths, a designation used when a person with confirmed measles dies within 30 days of developing symptoms, unless the death resulted from an unrelated event.

But Kennedy, a vaccine sceptic, has accused Shapiro of politicising the deaths and initially questioned whether two deaths reported by the state in August were linked to measles.

“The announcement appears to have been premature, and the deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers,” Kennedy wrote on the social media platform X on August 26.

Infectious disease experts warn that the dispute over how to classify the deaths puts the CDC at odds with a longstanding approach to tracking the consequences of measles. Epidemiologists have told Al Jazeera that tracking “measles-associated” deaths has long been a standard used by the World Health Organization and the CDC.

The latest death comes as Pennsylvania officials continue to seek additional federal assistance with the outbreak.

In its push for greater epidemiological support, the state requested an Epi-Aid investigation – used for urgent disease outbreaks and other disasters – from the CDC earlier this month, as cases continue to spread.

Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series was deadlocked at 3-3 Wednesday afternoon before Alec Bohm delivered Philadelphia's biggest swing. His two-out homer in the 10th inning lifted the Phillies to a 4-3 victory over the Atlanta Braves and forced a winner-take-all Game 3.

The Phillies had trailed 3-1 before Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper hit back-to-back homers in the seventh. Harper's blast came one inning after he committed a costly fielding error.

Playing under traditional extra-inning rules that don't include designated runners at second base like in the regular season, Bohm delivered his third career postseason home run, a 357-foot shot to right field off right-hander Didier Fuentes.

The Phillies will try to continue their postseason dominance over the Braves in Thursday's Game 3. Philadelphia beat Atlanta in the 1993 NLCS and the 2022 and 2023 NLDS.

Philadelphia Phillies’ Bryce Harper (3) reacts after hitting a home run against the Atlanta Braves during the eighth inning of Game 2 of the National League Wild Card Series at Truist Park on Sept. 30, 2026, in Atlanta, Ga. (Edward M. Pio Roda/Getty Images)

The Phillies pulled even with eighth-inning home runs by Schwarber and Harper off Dylan Lee, the winning pitcher in the Braves' 5-3 opening win on Tuesday. Schwarber’s drive carried 447 feet and Harper followed with a 418-foot drive.

articles.title: Anne Hathaway takes charge at the 'Verity' red carpet in viral moment
articles.excerpt:
The 43-year-old actress helped direct photographers while posing for the group photo at the New York premiere of her new movie, "Verity." (Video: Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

Anne Hathaway took cont...
articles.body_text:
The 43-year-old actress helped direct photographers while posing for the group photo at the New York premiere of her new movie, "Verity." (Video: Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

Anne Hathaway took control of the red carpet while at the premiere of her latest film.

While posing with the cast of her new film, "Verity," the 43-year-old actress calmly instructed photographers on how she planned on posing for their photos, in order to get the best shot possible.

In videos from the red carpet, Hathaway is heard telling the photographers where she will be looking and when, and tells the whole cast to follow suit.

The video from the premiere went viral on social media, with many fans praising her ability to get the photo taken efficiently.

Hathaway took the reins during a group photo on the red carpet at the "Verity" premiere. (Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images)

ANNE HATHAWAY, DAKOTA JOHNSON AND JOSH HARTNETT STAR IN R-RATED THRILLER ‘VERITY,’ OUT OCT 2

"Anne saw the group photo drifting and took the wheel immediately," one X user wrote, while another added, "She really said fine ill do it myself and honestly thats the energy every group photo needs."

Another fan took to the comments section on Facebook, writing, "Queen of Genovia knows best," with a fourth fan adding, "She's like "this dress and my ankles have a TIME LIMIT. let's make this EFFICIENT!!!"

Hathaway showed off her baby bump in a figure-hugging black mermaid gown designed by Prabal Gurung, which featured sequins, beading and a long sheer cape.

WATCH: Anne Hathaway directed photographers at the red carpet premiere of 'Verity'

This isn't the first time Hathaway has been recorded telling photographers what to do. A video of her greeting fans and paparazzi outside Valentino's fall 2022 show in Italy by telling them to "calma" went viral and became an audio trend, something Hathaway didn't expect.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Hathaway showed off her growing baby bump at the premiere of "Verity" in a black mermaid gown. (John Nacion/Variety via Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I remember that particular time, we were coming out of the pandemic so we were all feeling a little fragile," she told W Magazine in February 2024 about the viral video. "Like I said, so many of my fans learned about me when they were children. So their excitement comes from a pure place. I want them to know, I’m excited too. I feel like, if we can be calm in meeting each other, we’ll both be able to connect that much more significantly."

Hathaway is currently pregnant with her third child with her husband, Adam Shulman. The two tied the knot in September 2012 and share two sons; Jonathan and Jack.

The "Princess Diaries" star announced her third pregnancy on Instagram, in June, and debuted her baby bump on the red carpet at the world premiere of "The Odyssey" in London, England in July.

Her latest film, "Verity," which she stars in alongside Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett, is the fifth feature film the actress starred in this year. Her other films this year include "The End of Oak Street," "The Devil Wears Prada 2," "The Odyssey" and "Mother Mary."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Hathaway had five major projects premiere in 2026. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"It’s exciting, but it’s not like I planned it this way," she told The New Indian Express in August. "The five films are the proceeds of more than three years of work. It just so happens they are all out this year. Years ago, I would probably have been pretty stressed about that, but now I’m not. It’s fun to be here talking about films that I am so proud of."

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: In-laws charged with murder of New York Times games engineer in California
articles.excerpt:
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, charged days before Jonathan McKinsey and wife were set for hearing in divorce case

A California couple have been charged with murder after authorities say the...
articles.body_text:
Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, charged days before Jonathan McKinsey and wife were set for hearing in divorce case

A California couple have been charged with murder after authorities say they shot their son-in-law to death Saturday in a public park, days before he and the couple’s daughter were set for a hearing in a bitter divorce case.

Shili Chen and Shouyong Zhang, both 77, were due in court Wednesday for an arraignment on the charges. The Associated Press was not able to reach an attorney for the couple prior to the court appearance. Their daughter, Candice Jang, could not be reached, though she appeared virtually at Wednesday’s hearing.

Jonathan McKinsey, a 40-year-old gaming engineer for the New York Times, was shot dead in the parking lot of a sports complex in Dublin, east of San Francisco. A police sergeant was driving nearby and saw him on the ground as witnesses began calling 911 and pointing out the couple in their vehicle, who were still near the scene, Dublin police said in a news release.

Police detained the couple as they were driving away in the parking lot. Prosecutors said Zhang admitted to shooting McKinsey during a later interview, and a firearm was found in his car that he admitted to using during the crime.

Prosecutors also said surveillance video was recovered showing Chen and Zhang shooting the victim “in concert”.

Chen and Zhang’s murder charges included additional allegations of lying in wait and using a firearm.

Court records show McKinsey’s killing came during a contentious divorce with Jang and a custody battle over the couple’s three young children. In petitions for restraining orders filed last year, the couple accused each other of physical, emotional and psychological abuse going back more than a decade. McKinsey, who is transgender, alleged that both Jang and her parents were verbally and physically abusive regarding a gender transition he underwent years ago.

The killing occurred a week before a hearing was scheduled in McKinsey and Jang’s divorce case. The couple had been married since July 2011.

McKinsey joined the New York Times in January 2023. He was director of engineering for New York Times Games and based in the San Francisco Bay Area, the paper said. A spokesperson declined to comment further.

articles.title: Howard Stern warns ABC will have 'hell to pay' if something 'goes wrong' with Jimmy Kimmel's show
articles.excerpt:
Radio host Howard Stern said Tuesday there would be "hell to pay" at ABC should anything go wrong with Jimmy Kimmel's late-night show.

Radio host Howard Stern told the "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" audience o...
articles.body_text:
Radio host Howard Stern said Tuesday there would be "hell to pay" at ABC should anything go wrong with Jimmy Kimmel's late-night show.

Radio host Howard Stern told the "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" audience on Tuesday that ABC would have "hell to pay" if something went wrong with late-night host Jimmy Kimmel's show.

"I want to say something to ABC if they're watching right now," Stern said, noting he had previously heard rumors about the show and did not know what was true or not. "There is no man more loyal to this company than this guy."

"And what I mean by that, this is the truth. For years, I've said to him, you know, he goes to these things. ABC has a corporate function where they try to attract advertisers. Every year he'd go to what they call the upfronts," Stern said.

The radio host told the audience that Kimmel would always attend the events because ABC needed him to be there.

BOB IGER BREAKS SILENCE ON DISNEY'S SUSPENSION OF JIMMY KIMMEL OVER CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION COMMENTS

Radio host Howard Stern speaks with late-night host Jimmy Kimmel on Sept. 29, 2026. (ABC/JimmyKimmelLive)

"He has done everything for the company. And I hope that they keep that in mind," he said. "Oh my God. I don't know about you, but if something goes wrong, oh, is ABC going to have hell to pay. Am I correct? Are you with me?!"

ABC did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Reports of Kimmel's show being canceled were dismissed by ABC earlier this month. A spokesperson pushed back on Page Six's report that Kimmel's contract would not be renewed, calling any reports about the future of the late-night show "speculative."

"Howard Stern's reign as King of All Media is over in more ways than one," Hollywood in Toto founder Christian Toto told Fox News Digital in a statement about Stern's remarks. "The man who once stood tall for free speech went silent during the woke culture wars. Now, he's rushing to a multi-millionaire's defense, someone whose show is likely costing ABC dearly."

"That explains why the network needs a drastic budget reduction to keep ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live!’ on the air," he continued. "If CBS was losing $40 million a year to keep Stephen Colbert employed, imagine what ABC must swallow to appease Kimmel."

"The old Stern would have recognized those basic business principles," Toto added. "The new version? He's an ultra-rich liberal supporting a fellow ultra-rich liberal while misleading the public on the issues in play."

KIMMEL REVEALS HE'S INTERVIEWING JAMES TALARICO UNDER 'UNUSUAL CIRCUMSTANCES,' CITING FCC THREATS

Kimmel's show was taken off-air briefly in September 2025 after remarks the late-night host made about Charlie Kirk's assassin.

The liberal late-night personality returned to air a few days later, and has referenced the suspension in frequent jabs directed at President Donald Trump, as well as Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chair Brendan Carr.

Kimmel, after returning from his summer break on Sept. 8, jabbed at Carr and said, "We're still here."

The late-night host noted that it was the 4,000th episode of "Jimmy Kimmel Live!"

"We’ve done 4,000 of these. Which is, it’s a lot of shows," Kimmel said. "According to the White House, it’s too many shows."

"There are those who said we would never last this long. There are even those who used the regulatory might of the FCC to unconstitutionally try to make sure we didn’t last this long. But we did it the hard way, Brendan. And we are still here," Kimmel said.

DISNEY SUES FCC OVER ‘RETALIATORY CAMPAIGN AGAINST ABC,’ SEEKS TO BLOCK EARLY RENEWAL PROCEEDINGS

Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel hosting "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" on Monday, Sept. 28. (Disney via Getty Images)

The late-night host had New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on the show Monday night, and questioned him repeatedly about the nature of his relationship with Trump.

The democratic socialist mayor seemed to deflect Kimmel's questions as Mamdani avoided criticizing Trump and rejected the late-night host's request to send him a selfie.

"Did you guys hit it off immediately or is it something that you really went into thinking, like, ‘OK, I need to have a relationship with the president of the United States and I think the best way to do it is to charm him?' How did you do that and can you help me?" Kimmel asked Mamdani, calling his relationship with Trump "unexpected."

"The number one thing that we've been speaking about recently has been Sunnyside Yard, which is this idea for decades of building a platform over a rail yard and then building 12,000 homes. And so, in that moment, you know, that you zoomed in on, I'm just thinking about 12,000 homes, 30,000 jobs, largest housing development since the early 1970s," Mamdani told Kimmel.

Kimmel asked, "When you text him about Sunnyside, are you sure he doesn't think you're texting him about eggs?"

Mamdani said he was "pretty sure" and noted that the texts were pretty normal and didn't resemble the president's Truth Social posts.

"Wow. You really have broken through with him," Kimmel said. "I mean listen, you seem to be doing a great job in New York. We might need you to move to Washington just hang out at the Oval Office all day. Like if you texted him a selfie of us right now."

MAMDANI SAYS EVEN IF HE CAN GET ALONG WITH TRUMP, HE STILL DEMANDS THAT 'ICE SHOULD BE ABOLISHED'

"I love you, but I love housing more," Mamdani responded.

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.

articles.title: Pennsylvania reports fifth measles-related death of the year amid outbreak
articles.excerpt:
Measles outbreak in the state has now reached 39 counties, with 943 confirmed cases and 176 hospitalizations

Pennsylvania has reported its fifth measles-associated death of 2026 as the state’s ongoin...
articles.body_text:
Measles outbreak in the state has now reached 39 counties, with 943 confirmed cases and 176 hospitalizations

Pennsylvania has reported its fifth measles-associated death of 2026 as the state’s ongoing outbreak climbs to 943 confirmed cases across 39 counties.

The Pennsylvania department of health said on Wednesday that an unvaccinated Lancaster county resident who tested positive for measles had died. Health officials did not release further information about the individual, citing privacy protections.

The death marks the fifth Pennsylvania resident to meet the state’s definition of a measles-associated death this year after a fourth death two weeks ago. Due to how the Trump administration has changed its method for reporting measles deaths, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has not counted the Pennsylvania measles deaths in its national tally.

As of Monday, 28 September, Pennsylvania has recorded 40 new positive cases. The outbreak has now reached 39 counties, with 943 cumulative confirmed cases, 176 hospitalizations and five confirmed measles-associated deaths.

Only four of those confirmed cases have involved vaccinated individuals, representing less than 1% of the state’s total cases.

Health officials say daily totals can change, but monitoring the numbers gives residents and healthcare providers a clearer picture of community transmission across Pennsylvania and helps guide the state’s response.

Agricultural communities in Lancaster and Mifflin counties have remained at the center of Pennsylvania’s outbreak. Utah, Florida, Virginia and Texas have also reported dozens of cases, according to tracking from Johns Hopkins University.

Since the outbreak began in late April, staff at state health centers have administered more than 5,500 measles, mumps and rubella vaccine (MMR) vaccinations through 180 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities, according to a statement released Wednesday.

Dozens of additional vaccination clinics are planned for the coming weeks and months, depending on community interest and need, the statement added.

More than 3,600 measles cases have been reported across the US in 2026, according to the CDC. The US eliminated measles in 2000, though it is unclear whether it can retain that status amid the recent outbreaks.

Measles is considered one of the most contagious diseases known to medicine. The MMR vaccine prevents 97% of measles cases.

Vaccination rates among kindergarten-aged children, which are considered an important indicator, have slowly declined as experts argue the Trump administration is promoting confusion and misinformation about vaccines among parents.

Earlier this month, Pennsylvania requested emergency assistance from the CDC in response to the measles outbreak, but warned that the request could be withdrawn unless the federal agency publicly recognized the measles-associated deaths reported by the state.

The dispute began after Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary and former head of an anti-vaccine advocacy group, publicly questioned whether the deaths linked to the measles outbreaks since he took office were caused by the virus or by another condition.

articles.title: South Carolina mom accused of knife attack on young children; 6-year-old may lose arm: sheriff's office

articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A South Carolina boy’s call to his grandmother saying he was hungry led authorities to a home where investigators say his mother had stabbed him and his younger sibling dozens of times, leaving both children with severe injuries.

Taylor Gosnell, 35, is charged with two counts of attempted murder after allegedly attacking her children, ages 6 and 3, inside their Spartanburg County home during the overnight hours before they were discovered Saturday, according to authorities.

The 6-year-old called his grandmother Sept. 26, and told her his mother was not home and that he and his 3-year-old sibling were hungry, according to the Spartanburg County Sheriff’s Office.

ACCUSED NC KILLER MOM PLANS INSANITY DEFENSE — AS RETIRED JUDGE SAYS MORE MAY FOLLOW LINDSAY CLANCY STRATEGY

Taylor Gosnell, 35, is charged with two counts of attempted murder and two counts of possession of a weapon during a violent crime in Spartanburg County, S.C. (Spartanburg County Sheriff's Office)

The grandmother contacted a friend of Gosnell, and the two went to the residence. They found both children suffering from severe injuries and immediately dialed 911.

Deputies responding shortly after 2:30 p.m. found the residence in disarray, with numerous items damaged or broken, authorities said.

Investigators said the children suffered approximately 50 stab wounds between them, including injuries that penetrated to the bone. Both were initially taken to Spartanburg Regional Medical Center before being transferred to Prisma Health Children’s Hospital in Greenville, where they remained hospitalized and were expected to undergo additional surgeries.

SUBURBAN ILLINOIS BOY DIES IN SUSPECTED DOMESTIC HOMICIDE AS NEIGHBORS FEAR ANOTHER LINDSAY CLANCY CASE

Arrest warrants reviewed by Fox News Digital provide additional details about the alleged attack. The warrants allege Gosnell struck the children with a baseball bat and a circular knife, causing severe injuries, with intent to kill them.

Gosnell returned to the home while deputies were still at the scene, according to the sheriff’s office. Deputies transported her to Spartanburg Regional Medical Center for an evaluation after observing behavior that raised concerns about her immediate well-being.

Authorities said Gosnell attempted to run from the ambulance before being transported and had to be restrained. She was medically cleared and released from the hospital shortly afterward.

DAYS AFTER LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL, ANOTHER MASSACHUSETTS MOM ACCUSED OF KILLING HER CHILDREN SEEKS FREEDOM

Gosnell returned to the home while deputies were still at the scene. (Getty Images, File)

Investigators attempted to interview Gosnell, but no interview was conducted after she requested an attorney, according to the sheriff’s office.

Gosnell was booked into the Spartanburg County Detention Facility shortly before midnight Sept. 26, and was denied bond on both attempted murder charges.

Investigators later obtained two additional warrants charging Gosnell with possession of a weapon during a violent crime. Those warrants, also reviewed by Fox News Digital, allege she possessed the weapons during the attempted murders.

The children have been placed in protective custody and remain hospitalized, authorities said.

The investigation remains active and ongoing.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

FIRST LADY MELANIA TRUMP, FOX CORPORATION ANNOUNCE LANDMARK STRATEGIC ALLIANCE TO GROW FOSTERING THE FUTURE

articles.title: Trump DoJ indicts 10 individuals on noncitizen voting related charges in Minnesota
articles.excerpt:
The charges are senior officials’ latest attempt to heighten voter fraud concerns amid midterm election campaigning

The US Department of Justice indicted another 10 individuals on noncitizen voting r...
articles.body_text:
The charges are senior officials’ latest attempt to heighten voter fraud concerns amid midterm election campaigning

The US Department of Justice indicted another 10 individuals on noncitizen voting related charges on Wednesday as Donald Trump’s administration continues to pursue allegations of voter fraud raised by the president.

In the sixth announcement of its kind this month, the attorney general, Todd Blanche, and homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said 10 people in Minnesota were charged with making false claims about citizenship to vote, or voting as a noncitizen.

“Elections today are often decided by a small number of votes and that’s why these investigations and prosecutions matter,” Blanche told reporters during a press conference, in the latest bid by senior Trump officials to heighten concerns about voter fraud.

While there is no evidence that fraudulent voting is a substantial problem, Trump and his allies have repeatedly made unfounded allegations while claiming the electoral process is rigged against them. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative thinktank that often supports the administration’s initiatives, maintains a database of noncitizen voting – and identified 100 cases from 1982 to 2025. As the New York Times has noted, that represents 0.000008% of the 1.3bn votes cast in presidential elections over that period.

Mullin went further than Blanche on Wednesday, suggesting that voting machines were not secure. “We’ve had some trouble with some machines,” he said, without providing evidence, but adding: “Can’t say that it was fraud or not fraud.”

Administration officials have sought to support Trump’s longstanding unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud in US elections through investigations and indictments related to election concerns.

Trump has sought to undermine public confidence in US elections by promoting false claims of election fraud and making unverified claims of election insecurity. Earlier this year, the president heightened those claims in a primetime address.

The US president has also pushed through a crackdown on voting, ostensibly to secure elections – despite experts assuring voters that elections are already secure.

That includes directing his administration attempting to implement new rules to restrict mail-in ballot voting, a method of voting Trump has criticized, to create a federal database of eligible citizens and force voters to provide proof of citizenship when voting in federal elections.

Most of those actions have been challenged in court.

Noncitizen voting is rare and often associated with administrative errors. In a September 2o26 report, the Center for Election Innovation & Research found that “sweeping allegations about possible noncitizen registration or voting appear to arise from misunderstandings, mischaracterizations, or outright fabrications about complex voter data.”

Federal citizenship verification tools found that 0.04% of voter verification cases are returned as noncitizen, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.

Recently, New Jersey announced it found that more than 6,000 noncitizens had been falsely registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024, due to a system error. Of those, fewer than 340 voted.

Since early September, the DoJ has charged at least 24 individuals across 10 states with similar charges. In most of those cases, the individuals charged are lawful permanent residents.

The 10 individuals charged in Minnesota are all lawful permanent residents who either allegedly made false claims of citizenship to vote, or cast a ballot as a noncitizen, in the 2022 or 2024 general elections and 2026 primaries.

At least three of the Minnesota defendants have pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The Guardian has reached out to attorneys representing nine of the individuals indicted for comment. One defendant did not have an attorney listed on record.

An attorney for Alan Barbu Kargb, a Liberian national with lawful permanent resident status who was charged with noncitizen voting and making false claims about citizenship to vote, declined to comment.

articles.title: Stewart expects Schumer, Jeffries to disappoint if the Dems win back the House and Senate
articles.excerpt:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries holds a press availability on Capitol Hill. The New York Democrat addresses legislative priorities, economic concerns, and key party messaging.

Talk show host Jo...
articles.body_text:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries holds a press availability on Capitol Hill. The New York Democrat addresses legislative priorities, economic concerns, and key party messaging.

Talk show host Jon Stewart suggested that even if Democrats win a massive victory in the midterms, a future Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and a future Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., will turn out to be massive disappointments.

Democrats were initially in disarray after President Donald Trump’s victory against then-Vice President Kamala Harris in November. However, as Trump’s base fractured amid the Iran war and the affordability crisis that followed, Democrats are expected to win a historic victory in this November’s midterms.

On Wednesday, Stewart was asked a humorous question on his podcast about whether the downside of a Democratic midterm victory will be Schumer and Jeffries getting more "airtime."

"Look, I think what’s going to happen is they’re going to have to f---ing do something, they’re going to have to deliver," he said. "They’re not going to be able — it will not be sufficient to make their entire personalities opposition to whatever Trump politics are; they’re going to have to have a prescription for rebalancing this economy in a smart and urgent way."

JOHNSON DOWNPLAYS GOP'S MIDTERM WOES AS DEMOCRATS EYE HOUSE TAKEOVER: 'I AM VERY BULLISH'

Comedy Central host Jon Stewart suggested that even if there is a massive blue wave, as anticipated, Schumer and Jeffries will fail to utilize the power they gain. (Phillip Faraone / Getty)

"I am not confident that is in their DNA," Stewart continued. "I’m not confident that it’s in Schumer’s DNA, certainly, which means I’m actually hopeful he won’t be there as the leader. That they will come in and say, ‘We’re not going to go down that corporatist path again. We are going to make the changes that the American people are demanding that we make in an urgent way that is not bound by some idealized vision of what the parliamentarian might think is OK.’"

"F--- that," Stewart said. "Like, if you are granted control, if they give you the ring, do something with it, you b-----ds."

Fox News Digital contacted Jeffries and Schumer and did not receive an immediate reply.

HAKEEM JEFFRIES REJECTS MEDICARE FOR ALL, DSA AGENDA AS RO KHANNA CALLS HEALTH PLAN 'MOST IMPORTANT PRIORITY'

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital she agrees with Stewart's take."I agree with Jon Stewart that both Schumer and Jeffries are not confident leaders, but that’s because their ideology is power," she responded. "They are not the brakes that will restrain the Democratic Party from pursuing a radical agenda. Instead, they often appease the more radical members of their conference and push the party leftwards on issues like the courts, federal agencies, government spending, progressive prosecutors, and immigration whenever they have the votes."

"Both men have shown little willingness to challenge the party’s more extreme factions; for example, they have said they will welcome DSA candidates who win primaries into their ‘big tent’ party," she added. "They are not centrists; they follow the prevailing political winds within their party and will implement those policies to hold power, even if those policies run counter to what the American people support."Former Democratic advisor Dan Turrentine argued that Stewart's comments express the frustration Democratic voters have with party leaders."Voters are frustrated and angry that neither party is focused on them," he told Fox News Digital. "We are winning because Republicans are losing, not because we are doing things well. The D ‘Majority Makers’ are not going to be the progressive, base candidates, but moderates, who will want to focus on common-sense affordability issues, not the 'revenge' and ‘blow everything up’ base stuff. Jeffries and Schumer will need to balance this to protect their majority while maintaining base enthusiasm. It is a ‘both’ and not ‘either/or’ scenario. Given how weak both are, and that they both will face a primary challenge next year, it is going to be tough."

He added, "I think Stewart is indicative of the irrational expectations of the base. They don’t appreciate the different reasons different people are angry. We are not potentially winning in IA, AK, KS, TX, SC, for the same reasons DSA candidates are winning."

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks to the media next to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: Inside Diddy's prison life with massages, booze and nude photos: report
articles.excerpt:
Fox News' CB Cotton and trial attorney Kelly Hyman join 'Fox News Live' to discuss a proposal for the release of music mogul Sean 'Diddy' Combs from his 50-month prison sentence and more.

Sean "Diddy...
articles.body_text:
Fox News' CB Cotton and trial attorney Kelly Hyman join 'Fox News Live' to discuss a proposal for the release of music mogul Sean 'Diddy' Combs from his 50-month prison sentence and more.

Sean "Diddy" Combs may be behind bars, but he has reportedly found a way to bring the perks of his former luxury lifestyle with him.

Combs, who is serving out his 50-month sentence at Fort Dix in New Jersey, has essentially hired a full staff within the prison walls, NBC News reported. Four men living in the same unit as the disgraced music mogul spoke to the outlet about the unusual comforts Combs has secured behind bars.

"He’s a billionaire. People are in awe of him," one of the anonymous sources told the outlet. "Money is power, especially behind bars."

DIDDY SENT TO SOLITARY CONFINEMENT AFTER PRISON FIGHT WITH ANOTHER INMATE: MULTIPLE REPORTS

Sean "Diddy" Combs has reportedly recreated many of the comforts of his former luxury lifestyle while serving his 50-month prison sentence at Fort Dix, with fellow inmates allegedly making his bed, cooking meals, doing laundry and giving him massages. (Mark Mainz/Getty Images)

From freshly made beds to cooked meals, clean laundry and Chinese-style massages, Diddy has reportedly turned fellow inmates into a makeshift prison staff.

"This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---," one of the men told NBC. "It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy."

Contraband cellphones, explicit photos, prescription pills and premium booze — Combs’ alleged prison perks reportedly extend well beyond his makeshift staff.

Sources told NBC News the music mogul uses illicit phones to scroll Instagram and view nude and sexually explicit photos sent by an ex-girlfriend. He has also allegedly purchased Remeron, an antidepressant dubbed "rem-roms" behind bars, from other inmates for its mood-boosting effects.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Sean "Diddy" Combs also allegedly has access to contraband cellphones, explicit photos, prescription pills, premium liquor and a modified tablet to watch movies, according to inmates who spoke with NBC News. (Jane Rosenberg)

On weekend nights, Combs would reportedly break into a secret stash of top-shelf liquor allegedly smuggled into the prison by guards and shared with a small circle of inmates.

"You can pretty much get anything except a key to the front door and a female," one of the sources said.

Diddy had even gotten his hands on a "jailbroken" tablet to watch movies – including "Sean Combs: The Reckoning," produced by 50 Cent – according to the men.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Sean "Diddy" Combs' representative denied the reports to Fox News Digital, arguing that media attention has exaggerated ordinary prison life and insisting the rapper continues to follow prison rules while awaiting a decision on his appeal. (Scott Dudelson)

Combs’ representative pushed back on the portrayal of his life behind bars, dismissing the attention surrounding his day-to-day routine as overblown.

"The continued scrutiny of every mundane detail of Sean Combs’s life in prison has reached the point where the media characterizes ordinary prison life as news," Diddy's rep told Fox News Digital. "The only real news is that Sean continues to serve his sentence within the rules, and he patiently awaits the court’s decision on his appeal."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Sean "Diddy" Combs was sentenced in October 2025 after being acquitted of sex-trafficking and racketeering charges, and he is currently appealing his sentence while serving time with a projected release date of Jan. 21, 2028. (Jane Rosenberg)

Fox News Digital reached out to Fort Dix for comment.

The musician was sentenced on Oct. 3, 2025 to 50 months behind bars, followed by five years of supervised release and a $500,000 fine. The rapper was transferred to Fort Dix to serve out the rest of his sentence later that month. As of publication, Diddy's release date was set as Jan. 21, 2028.

Diddy's eight-week trial, during which jurors heard dozens of witness testimonies, concluded on July 2, 2025. The rapper was acquitted on the most serious charges against him – sex-trafficking and racketeering.

The "I'll Be Missing You" singer has filed an appeal. Diddy's team claimed the sentence handed down to him was illegal because the judge relied on charges the jury rejected, according to the appeal briefing obtained by Fox News Digital.
