articles.title: Tennessee halts plan to execute woman for first time in 200 years
articles.excerpt:
State governor and supreme court earlier refused calls for clemency for Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder

Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years was halted by a court on Wednesda...
articles.body_text:
State governor and supreme court earlier refused calls for clemency for Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder

Tennessee’s first execution of a woman in 200 years was halted by a court on Wednesday morning an hour before it was set to take place.

The state governor and the supreme court had earlier refused calls for clemency in the case of Christa Pike, who was convicted of murder 30 years ago.

She was set to die by lethal injection at 11am ET on Wednesday but the execution has been halted by a federal appeals court.

In a 2-1 majority, the court said: “The interests of justice and the finality of Pike’s impending execution compel the entry of a short stay of execution in order to properly analyze the parties’ fully briefed arguments and resolve the issues on the merits.”

The office of Jonathan Skrmetti, the state attorney general, issued a statement reacting to the news on Wednesday, saying: “We will continue to advocate for the lawfully imposed sentence as the courts work through this technical issue. It is common in capital cases for the defense to raise last-minute objections following decades of litigation in numerous courts. We are asking the supreme court of the United States to lift the stay.”

The Guardian has reached out to the office of Bill Lee, Tennessee’s Republican governor.

Pike, who is now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend, who was 17 at the time, killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, one of their classmates at Knoxville Job Corps in 1995.

The case garnered nationwide headlines due to the ages of everyone involved, as well as a satanic symbol that was carved into Slemmer’s chest.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: Photos: Kashmir’s 600-year-old Wazwan wedding feast adapts to modern life
articles.excerpt: As autumn approaches, the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb echoes across courtyards and back lanes in Kashmir, where cooks prepare Wazwan – a lavish, multi-course mutton feast that remain...
articles.body_text:
As autumn approaches, the rhythmic thud of wooden mallets pounding lamb echoes across courtyards and back lanes in Kashmir, where cooks prepare Wazwan – a lavish, multi-course mutton feast that remains central to traditional wedding celebrations.

Wazwan arrived in the valley from Central Asia in the 14th century, when rulers brought skilled chefs along with the carpet and shawl weavers that later defined the region’s craft heritage.

Today, the feast is both a marker of social status and a powerful symbol of Kashmiri identity.

Among its guardians is 74-year-old Ghulam Nabi Baba, a veteran Wazwan chef who traces his lineage to those early migrants. His forefathers settled in Srinagar’s old city as part of a community of cooks known as Wazpora.

“There were only seven mutton dishes at that time. Over the centuries we added more, and now there are around 20,” Baba said.

He explained how the number of dishes and the amount of meat often reflect a family’s wealth.

“Forty years ago in Delina [a village in north Kashmir] I cooked 4,500kg (9,920 pounds) of meat. That was a very big wedding. Normally, at an average marriage we cook 200kg (440 pounds),” he added.

Despite the expanding menu, the core techniques have changed little. Lightly spiced meat is still pounded by hand before being simmered slowly over wood fires – a labour-intensive process Baba has followed since joining his father as a cook at 15.

But the pressures of modern life are reshaping the tradition. Baba’s son has chosen to open a restaurant rather than work weddings, saying the round-the-clock demands are too exhausting.

He believes he is still carrying forward the family’s centuries-old culinary legacy – just in a different setting, as Wazwan adapts to contemporary tastes and lifestyles.

articles.title: We need ‘right to intervene’ in AI amid growing threat, says Bank of England boss
articles.excerpt:
Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage

The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid g...
articles.body_text:
Andrew Bailey’s comments come as fears grow that rogue models could take financial system hostage

The governor of the Bank of England has called for the “right to intervene” in the AI industry amid growing fears that rogue models could take the financial system hostage.

Andrew Bailey said the risks posed by frontier AI models – a number of which have gone rogue in recent months – were “real and increasingly significant”. Meanwhile, it was becoming harder for the public to have proper oversight of powerful AI models that were “functioning within a self-reinforcing loop”.

That is putting financial stability at risk, with the new technology having increased the “scale and sophistication of cyber threats to the financial system”, he said. The governor warned it could threaten daily card payments, bank transactions, and stock and bond trading across financial markets.

The comments came as the Bank’s financial policy committee (FPC) said the growing mountain of AI debt was increasing financial stability risks.

The potential benefits of AI “are immense”, Bailey said but he added that authorities needed to be ready to step in.

In an opinion piece penned for the Bank of England’s Insight series, he said: “If we are to realise those benefits safely, we must answer one critical question. Should society retain the ability to intervene, to establish the boundaries within which these systems operate and to revise those boundaries as the technology evolves? To my mind, the answer is unequivocally yes.”

But Bailey said authorities needed to figure out why they might be forced to step in. He said a “sensible starting point” would be rigorous testing of new AI models to understand how they behave and identify “credible points” where authorities could intervene.

“In time, that understanding could be codified into a set of standards which will help to ensure consistency in approach across the financial system, and perhaps more broadly across the economy,” he said.

However, the governor stopped short of calling for a regulatory clampdown, saying it was “not, in my view, the right place to start. In the excitement surrounding AI development, there is a risk that we move too quickly to debates about regulatory architecture before establishing where the failure exists in the first place.”

A growing number of lawmakers, AI researchers and even some AI companies have called for more government oversight of artificial intelligence in recent weeks. However, hopes for international cooperation faded after Donald Trump broadly rejected calls for more regulation of AI technology – most of which is being developed in the US – warning it could hurt efforts to compete with China and threaten economic growth.

But Bailey said a set of standards could help safeguard the financial system from harmful AI, which may end up operating outside well-established “shared norms, obligations and responsibilities”.

“Central banks have a responsibility to safeguard the stability of the system as a whole,” Bailey said. “We cannot stand aside and assume that technological progress will resolve these questions on its own. The public interest requires that we engage with them now, before the risks become more difficult to contain.”

Warning of the ballooning AI debt pile, the FPC said large players in the sector had taken on $450bn (£339bn) worth of debt between January and September this year, already overtaking the $333bn worth of gilts due to be issued by the UK government for the whole of 2026.

That has tied investors – including hedge funds, asset managers and private credit firms – to the fortunes of AI companies at a time when those tech businesses have yet to turn a profit.

“The rapid increase in artificial intelligence-related debt issuance broadens the exposure of capital markets to development in AI,” minutes of the recent FPC meeting on 25 September said.

“The committee underscores the importance of timely and careful management of these intensifying, interconnected risks.”

articles.title: WNBA refs miss opportunity to eject A'ja Wilson over meltdown, entering stands
articles.excerpt:
Dan Dakich thinks the lights are a little too bright for A'ja Wilson.

Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson only received a technical foul on Tuesday night when she stepped across the baseline and went a f...
articles.body_text:
Dan Dakich thinks the lights are a little too bright for A'ja Wilson.

Las Vegas Aces star A’ja Wilson only received a technical foul on Tuesday night when she stepped across the baseline and went a few rows deep to address an Indiana Fever fan.

The incident occurred in the fourth quarter of the Aces’ Game 2 loss to the Fever at the Gainbridge Fieldhouse. Wilson drew a blocking foul after Sophie Cunningham stepped in front of her and fell to the court. Cunningham was upset with the call, meanwhile, Wilson was seen yelling and pointing at a fan a few rows from courtside.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson talks to teammates after going into the stands to confront a fan during Game 2 of the first round of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs against the Indiana Fever at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

The broadcast showed Wilson taking a few steps into the stands. Crew chief Randy Richardson was asked by a pool reporter about the incident.

"So, at that point, A’ja Wilson was assessed a technical foul for unsportsmanlike conduct," Richardson told the reporter when asked what happened with the incident.

When asked, "Why did A’ja Wilson receive a tech for her interaction with the fan on the baseline," Richardson responded, "For unsportsmanlike conduct."

Wilson finished the game, but it appeared the incident may have warranted an ejection.

The league considers the stands the first row of seats. Wilson didn’t climb over anyone to get to the fan she had an issue with, but, on the baseline, she didn’t need to.

"Any coach, player, or trainer who deliberately enters the spectator stands during the game will be automatically ejected and the incident reported via e-mail to the Commissioner," the rulebook states.

OutKick asked the WNBA and National Basketball Referees Association for comment on why Wilson’s action didn’t warrant an ejection. OutKick also asked the WNBA if it would review the incident further.

The Fever released a statement on the incident.

"Following a report of a comment directed toward a player, arena security spoke with the fan involved and witnesses," the team said. "Security determined there was no violation of the Fan Code of Conduct, the fan was not removed from the arena. We consider the matter closed."

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson talks to a referee after going into the stands to confront a fan during Game 2 of the first round of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs against the Indiana Fever at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Wilson addressed the confrontation after the game.

"If I see a man, come at me, taking steps toward me and point at me, I don’t give a damn what you said, I don’t give a damn how you said it, the tone, that is unacceptable," she said. "You don’t step toward me and point at me. I’m not for that s--- at all.

"That’s unacceptable and how he gets back in the game because they said he didn’t know anything, of course he didn’t, and that’s fine. And I apologized to my team because I got us a tech and I didn’t … but there’s certain things I’m just not gonna allow anymore because it’s just unacceptable. You don’t know me at all to come and step toward me and point at me and say anything."

A fan sitting next to the man in question later told OutKick that the man only said the foul was on Wilson and pointed at her.

As the WNBA has grown more popular, the scrutiny over officiating in the league has come under the microscope and this season was no different.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert said last summer the league was going to evolve terms of its officiating. The league formed an offseason officiating task force that included an effort to clean up some of the WNBA’s issues regarding physicality and officiating.

Minnesota Lynx head coach Cheryl Reeve, who blasted officials during last year’s WNBA Finals, said in the beginning of the 2026 season that coaches weren’t looking for referees to call marginal fouls.

New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart and Dallas Wings rookie Azzi Fudd also talked about the fouls. Stewart was annoyed that a game against the Washington Mystics earlier in the year took nearly three hours to complete. Fudd was dismayed about being unable to be physical with opponents.

Fever star Caitlin Clark went as far as to call for full-time WNBA referees as she racked up technical fouls this season that nearly cost her a game.

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson holds the ball while Indiana Fever center Aliyah Boston defends during Game 2 of the first round of the 2026 WNBA Playoffs at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on Sept. 29, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"It's kind of been a discussion for three years now, and I think we really need to do a better job protecting the people in this league," she said in July. "I've been involved in a few of those plays, but there's been plenty of others across the league that haven't been called. You go back postgame or whatever it is, teams submit clips and nothing changes. I think overall the league has to do better."

"Overall, the league just has to do better and we have to invest in those areas," she added. "The technology can get better. We can treat the referees a little bit better. Pay them like they're full-time employees."

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

With the rules already in place, one has to wonder why Wilson wasn’t ejected from Tuesday night’s game.

OutKick’s Amber Harding contributed to this report.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: GOP fortress is under threat in one key red state, and these voters could decide whether it falls
articles.excerpt:
Voters at the State Fair discuss whether Talarico can defeat Ken Paxton, turn Texas blue and end Democrats’ decadeslong statewide losing streak.

DALLAS — A competitive Senate race is testing whether ...
articles.body_text:
Voters at the State Fair discuss whether Talarico can defeat Ken Paxton, turn Texas blue and end Democrats’ decadeslong statewide losing streak.

DALLAS — A competitive Senate race is testing whether Texas is still safely red, with Black and Hispanic voters at the center of Democrat James Talarico's path to victory.

Talarico is seeking to become the first Democrat in more than 30 years to win a statewide race in the Lone Star State.

"I definitely do think, if there’s any time for Texas to get a Democrat elected, this is the time to strike," Mike, a military veteran from Dallas, told Fox News Digital. "I think it depends on whether the Black and Brown voters come out for Talarico."

POLL: TALARICO TIES PAXTON IN TEXAS SENATE RACE, THREATENING GOP STRONGHOLD

Texas voters Mike and Kiara discuss the importance of Black voter turnout and the possibility of Democrat James Talarico flipping the state in the Nov. 3 Senate election at the State Fair in Dallas on Sept. 29. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

"Everyone says, ‘Hey, we are Texas and we want change here, we want change there,’" Mike added. "Well, this is an opportunity for you guys to get change. Are you going to come out and show up at the polls? He’s got all the momentum in the world. He’s got everything going for him."

Mike’s comments reflect the challenge facing Talarico as he works to build support among Black and Hispanic voters and motivate them to turn out in November.

Texas has more Black eligible voters than any other state, with roughly 2.7 million. That puts voters in Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth and East Texas in a potentially decisive position in any Democrat’s bid to win statewide.

Former President Barack Obama’s appearance with Talarico at a May campaign stop in Austin underscored the stakes for Democrats to leverage a massive voting bloc in Texas. The party's effort to win over Black voters could help determine whether Texas remains reliably red or becomes more competitive for Democrats in future elections.

TEXAS VOTERS HAVE PLENTY TO SAY ABOUT WHETHER LONE STAR STATE COULD TURN BLUE

Former President Barack Obama joined Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico at a campaign stop in Austin in May, as Talarico works to build support among Black voters in Texas. (Joel Angel Juarez/Pool/Getty Images)

But Talarico faces an uphill battle in uniting Democrats behind his campaign after a divisive primary against Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas. Talarico defeated Crockett in the Democratic primary earlier this year, and the outgoing congresswoman has not endorsed his Senate campaign.

Crockett has said she supports the Democratic ticket in Texas, but her political action committee has not endorsed Talarico or campaigned for him.

Rashaun, of Forney, Texas, said the primary loss may have left some Black voters frustrated.

"Everyone was behind Jasmine," Rashaun said. "So that’s what’s blocking, I’m going to say for my people, that was blocking their minds."

Still, Rashaun said she plans to vote for Talarico and hopes Texas will turn blue in November.

"Yes, we are voting in November and it’s going to be Talarico," she said. "We need Texas to flip. We can wish and hope and pray. But we need to get out and vote."

TEXAS VOTERS HAVE PLENTY TO SAY ABOUT WHETHER LONE STAR STATE COULD TURN BLUE

Black voters are a crucial part of any Democrat’s path to statewide victory in Texas, which has the nation’s largest Black electorate. (Mark Felix/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Mike said the election may ultimately come down to whether voters are willing to act.

"Right now it is on the Texas voters to get out and support James Talarico or sit at home if you don’t want to see that change," he said.

Bryant, of Coppell, Texas, likewise pointed to frustration with Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton, both Republicans, as a potential motivator for people to support Talarico's candidacy.

"This is a critical election," Bryant said. "I think we all can feel it in Texas, the need to get Greg Abbott out."

REPUBLICANS JUST GOT A POWERFUL NEW PLAYBOOK FOR THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS. HERE'S WHAT'S INSIDE

Bryant, a Coppell resident, shared his perspective on the closely watched U.S. Senate race and the state’s political future at the Texas State Fair in Dallas on Sept. 29, 2026. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

"It’s time for a change," he added. "Plus, on the other side, you see how bad Ken Paxton is and his track record and just some of the things that he’s done. It’s no longer working and we need to do something different."

Ava, a college student from Denton, said Talarico’s outreach to younger voters has helped him connect with a generation that often feels overlooked.

"I do think he’s going to pull through," she said. "He engages with the younger community, which is important because we feel like we’re not represented."

She added that his social media presence has also helped younger voters connect with his campaign. She first learned about Talarico after meeting him at the Texas State Fair last year and later followed him online.

Ava, a college student from Denton, said Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico has resonated with younger Texas voters and could help flip the state blue. (Amanda Macias/Fox News Digital)

While Ava focused on Talarico’s appeal among younger voters, Kiara, of Dallas, said supporters must turn that enthusiasm into votes.

"I live in Texas, and I’ve been here for a really long time, and it’s time for a change, a positive change," she said. "And I think Talarico is definitely going to bring that."

"We just have to vote," Kiara added. "We can’t complain about the problems if you don’t want to vote to fix them."

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

articles.title: Pilot who stabbed co-pilot on Israel-bound plane may have tried to crash it, says Netanyahu
articles.excerpt:
Israeli officials investigating if incident, which forced plane to make emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, was attempted terror attack

One of the pilots of a plane flying from the UAE to Israel stabb...
articles.body_text:
Israeli officials investigating if incident, which forced plane to make emergency landing in Saudi Arabia, was attempted terror attack

One of the pilots of a plane flying from the UAE to Israel stabbed his co-pilot and appeared to try  to crash the plane, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said, as Israeli officials said they were investigating if the incident was an attempted terror attack on Israelis.

The plane was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after the apparent attack, with the two pilots wounded but other passengers safe, according to a statement by Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz international airport, more commonly known as Tabuk airport.

The pilot accused of carrying out the attack was currently being questioned by Saudi authorities, Netanyahu said.

The Israeli defence minister, Israel Katz, described the incident as an “attempted jihadist attack”. “The terrorist had a single objective: to crash the plane, killing everyone onboard,” Katz said, adding that the attack was stopped due to the “heroism of several passengers”.

Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national and that Israel’s current assessment of the incident was that it was a terror attack. There was no comment on the attack from either Oman or the United Arab Emirates.

Two and a half hours after taking off from Dubai, the plane sent out an emergency signal – squawk code 7700, indicating a general emergency – before sending out another – code 7500, indicating a potential hijacking attempt.

The plane also abruptly descended, falling about 17,000 ft in a two-minute span, before diverting from Jordanian airspace towards Tabuk airport, in north-western Saudi Arabia, where it landed safely. Israeli officials told Reuters that the cabin crew took control of the cockpit and helped land the plane after the attack.

Videos of the incident showed passengers screaming as the plane descended, as well as a blood-covered man who appeared to be the pilot injured and on the floor.

“The co-pilot tried to murder the pilot and basically carry out a suicide attack on the plane,” passenger Miryam Shira Ohayon told reporters via her mother’s phone at Tel Aviv airport.

“It was really on the way to crashing, and it was simply the resourcefulness of many people who took control of the co-pilot and neutralised him,” she said, adding that a doctor on board treated the wounded pilot.

Israeli officials’ initially scrambled fighter jets after the emergency signals were sent out, fearing an attack on Israel or that the plane would be diverted to a third country. A spokesperson for the Israeli prime minister’s office then said the incident was not a hijacking, as media reports circulated of a fight between the two pilots.

As more information emerged about the violent nature of the attack, Israeli and international media began to report officials anonymously saying an investigation had been opened into whether this was an attack on Israelis.

Israeli authorities have so far refrained from publicly calling the alleged attack a suspected terror incident, besides the far-right national security minister. Itamar Ben-Gvir. Ben-Gvir said on X that “terrorism is a devil with whom no agreement must be reached”, referring to the incident.

The head of the Israeli military, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, postponed his planned visit to the US next week over the incident, where he was meant to have a meeting with US joint chiefs of staff and the head of US Central Command.

The circumstances of the brawl between the pilots were unclear, with passengers recounting confusing moments and blood being spilt.

Yasmin Abu Kaiss, whose daughter was on the flight, told Reuters her daughter said she had heard screaming and a man with a knife had put a pilot on the floor, and that there was blood everywhere.

Pictures published by Israeli media showed a passenger wearing a blood-soaked shirt. The Guardian could not independently verify the image.

The incident came just days after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, warned there were indications an attack would be carried out during Israel’s October elections. The Israeli military, quoted by Israeli media, said it had no intelligence that an attack was being planned on Israel.

Yair Lapid, an opposition figure and former prime minister, cast doubt on the connection between the alleged attack and Netanyahu’s warning, saying that a security briefing on Tuesday night gave no information about a possible incident similar to what happened on Wednesday.

Israel experienced a series of hijackings and attacks on planes by Palestinian militants in the 1960s and 1970s, but has not had anything similar in decades. The country maintains some of the strictest airport security procedures in the world, including security checks before passengers board Israel-bound flights.

Flights between Dubai and Israel started after the countries normalised ties in 2020. Israel does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, but in 2025 landed a plane in Riyadh because of a medical emergency.

Flydubai confirmed that flight FZ 1073 en route to Ben Gurion experienced an incident and landed safely in Tabuk on Wednesday. “Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities,” the carrier said. “Further updates will be issued as additional confirmed details become available.”

Israeli media reported that a later flydubai flight heading to Tel Aviv turned around in mid-air back towards Dubai after the incident.

articles.title: Israel-bound flight diverted after fight between pilots
articles.excerpt:
The Flydubai plane took off early on Wednesday morning (Stock photo)

A flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was unexpectedly diverted to Saudi Arabia after a fight between the pilots, Israeli officials told...
articles.body_text:
The Flydubai plane took off early on Wednesday morning (Stock photo)

A flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv was unexpectedly diverted to Saudi Arabia after a fight between the pilots, Israeli officials told local media.

The Flydubai plane - which took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates early on Wednesday morning - signalled an emergency code two hours into the journey, flight tracking website Flightradar24 said.

Minutes later it switched to a code used to report a hijacking, but was later turned back to the general emergency signal, it added.

The Israeli prime minister's office said the incident was not believed to have been a hijacking.

Passengers told local media they feared or their lives as the plane started to drop during the incident.

The emergency signal is thought to be issued following an altercation between the pilot and co-pilot, local media reported citing Israeli defence officials.

Flight FZ1073 - carrying around 150 people, most of whom are Israeli - was due to land at Ben-Gurion Airport but instead landed at Tabuk Airport in northeastern Saudi Arabia.

A Flydubai spokesperson confirmed the flight "experienced an incident while en route", and that updates will be issued as further details become available. "Our teams are working closely with the relevant authorities," it added.

Data from Flightrader24 shows a rapid descent for the plane over Saudi Arabia, just two hours after take-off, descending more than 17,000 feet (over 5000 m) in less than two minutes just after 05:21 UTC (06:21 BST).

At 05:40, the flight briefly entered Jordanian airspace before looping back into Saudi Arabia minutes later, where it then began its descent for landing.

The Israeli air force dispatched fighter jets in response to the incident and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held urgent consultations on the incident.

articles.title: New Orleans judge files criminal case against CBS affiliate over reporting
articles.excerpt:
Kimya Holmes’ lawsuit over a news segment on a real-estate transaction invokes law that no longer exists

A New Orleans state court judge filed a police complaint against a local CBS affiliate after i...
articles.body_text:
Kimya Holmes’ lawsuit over a news segment on a real-estate transaction invokes law that no longer exists

A New Orleans state court judge filed a police complaint against a local CBS affiliate after it aired a segment scrutinizing a real-estate transaction in which she was involved, with the jurist invoking a section of law that no longer carries criminal penalties, according to the journalist who reported the story.

The situation centering on New Orleans criminal court judge Kimya Holmes and investigative reporter David Hammer was only the latest in a series of high-profile matters pitting Louisiana journalists against members of the state’s court system.

Deputies at the New Orleans criminal courthouse handcuffed Hammer’s WWL Louisiana colleague, investigative producer Danny Monteverde, and an attorney for their station – Elana Beiser – in early July while the outlet covered an indictment filed against the state’s attorney general, which was ultimately dismissed.

And in August, a state court jury awarded a $300,000 verdict to Louisiana supreme court justice Jeff Hughes, who sued the Advocate newspaper for libel over an editorial – an outcome some US press freedom defenders fear could weaken the “actual malice” legal standard which has long governed such cases.

Hammer, whose channel is a Guardian reporting partner, published a 24 August story exploring how a $765,000 home was donated to Holmes in 2025 by a man to whom she was engaged at the time.

Holmes’ then-fiancee, accountant Arthur Allen, had been criminally charged weeks earlier with fraudulently collecting more than $712,000 in Covid-19 pandemic relief that was taxpayer-funded.

The judge told Hammer she didn’t start dating or become engaged to Allen until four years after he had committed the crime for which he was charged. She maintained she didn’t learn about his charges until close to the time he pleaded guilty in April – after the couple had broken up.

Hammer’s report on Holmes, Allen and the gated community home he donated to her – in which she continued to live while he paid the mortgage – arrived as she prepared for a tough 3 November re-election race against a fellow judge whose section of court was eliminated by a new law.

And on 10 September, a little more than two weeks after Hammer’s story, the New Orleans criminal courthouse’s judicial administrator sent WWL a letter demanding it remove a public record showing the address of the house Allen gave Holmes, the outlet reported on Tuesday.

Judicial administrator Robert Kazik’s letter furthermore demanded that WWL remove images of the license plate number of a Corvette leased by Allen that had been photographed by a station source while it was parked in the courthouse garage in August. Kazik’s letter also requested that WWL reveal who photographed the Corvette.

Kazik’s letter cited a Louisiana law that gave “third parties” including the news media three days to unpublish certain kinds of personal information about a judge once a judicial administrator requested it. It also made violations of that law a misdemeanor crime punishable by up to 90 days’ imprisonment and a $1,000 fine.

Yet the Louisiana legislature repealed both the portions of the law requiring news outlets to remove published information and making it a misdemeanor if they don’t do so. Those repeals took effect on 1 August – before Hammer’s reporting on Holmes’ donated house as well as Kazik’s letter.

Hammer reported on Tuesday that WWL reacted to Kazik’s letter by having videos with the information that the judicial administrator mentioned taken offline on the morning of 11 September. The outlet reposted them later with the address and license plate numbers blurred.

Nonetheless, WWL said it refused to disclose who photographed the Corvette. And on 11 September, Holmes filed a criminal complaint with the New Orleans police department (NOPD) against WWL for allegedly “revealing her home address and vehicle information”.

The outlet sought comment on the police complaint from New Orleans media lawyer Scott Sternberg, who lobbied for the repeals that took effect in the beginning of August.

Sternberg, who represented the Advocate newspaper against the state supreme court justice Hughes, said he believed the repeals were necessary because those portions were “wildly unconstitutional”, with press freedom being a fundamental US right.

“I can’t imagine a public official filing a criminal complaint in response to reporting that, based on my own opinion of it, seems to be accurate,” Sternberg remarked. “I mean – it was a real estate transaction.”

Hammer confirmed that the accuracy of his reporting on Holmes and Allen was never challenged, prompting Sternberg to say “it wouldn’t warrant a criminal complaint” even if it had been inaccurate.

Sternberg added that neither Kazik’s letter nor the police complaint “had any force or effect and that’s probably why … NOPD isn’t coming down here to arrest you – because there hasn’t been a crime”.

Hammer said WWL asked Holmes’ campaign spokesperson what the legal basis of the criminal complaint against the station was. The outlet also asked if Holmes knew that her complaint relied on a section of law that was no longer on the books.

The spokesperson replied with an email forwarded by Holmes that in part had an out-of-date version of the relevant law attached to it. That version of the law – still carrying the criminal penalties – came from Louisiana’s legislative website which had not been updated according to records from the state legislature’s most recent session.

A state legislature spokesperson told WWL that updating laws on the legislative website can take “many months”. The spokesperson also pointed to a website disclaimer which made “no guarantee … to its accuracy” – and said “these provisions and annotations have not been edited for publication and are not official or authoritative”.

The email which Holmes forwarded originally came from state appellate court judge Tiffany Gautier Chase on 26 August, two days after Hammer’s report on the house donated by Allen. Chase’s email notified judges of “protections against the dissemination of certain personal information”.

WWL reported that its attorney, Mary Ellen Roy, wrote to the NOPD to make sure the detective assigned to Holmes’ complaint was aware of the updated law.

Roy also wrote to the NOPD that WWL expected the detective’s investigation into the judge’s complaint “to be closed, forthwith”.

The NOPD said on Tuesday that its investigation into WWL was continuing.

articles.title: Burnham says UK ‘can’t afford another decade of post-Brexit drift’ as he leaves door open to rejoining the EU – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
The PM says all ‘the options’ being considered and calls for an open debate about the UK’s future relationship with Europe

Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EU

Burnham wants to re...
articles.body_text:
The PM says all ‘the options’ being considered and calls for an open debate about the UK’s future relationship with Europe

Andy Burnham: UK could ‘go all the way’ by rejoining EU

Burnham wants to review the UK’s relationship with the EU. What are the options?

From Brexit to electoral reform: key takeaways from Andy Burnham’s conference speech

In his Today interview, Andy Burnham also said that he thought Britain needed to resolve what its relationship with the EU should be because it could not afford another decade of drift.

double quotation markWhat I am saying is it’s not good enough to leave that question just hanging.

I am saying, let’s be clear about where we want Britain to go in the next decade. And I’ve asked people to join with me on that.

The country cannot have a decade, another one like the one we’ve just had, where we’ve had too much drift, too much division.

I am very clear, and I will say this bluntly, Brexit has caused more harm than good and I think around 60% of the British public agree with that statement.

So the question is what do we do about that?

And I’m not doing the usual politician thing. I’m being honest about facing up to that, and give people options that they can look at and judge.

Andy Burnham has said that he has spent “a lot of time” working out how to fill the £4.7bn gap in the plans to fund the defence investment plan.

When Keir Starmer unveiled the defence investment plan in June, after he had announced he was standing down to make way for Burnham, he said the increased investment would cost £15bn. While explaining where most of the money would come from, he said the remaining funds – worth £4.7bn over four years – would have to come from savings to be announced in the budget.

In an interview on Times Radio, Burnham said that finding this money had been a “major priority”.

double quotation markI said as soon as I came in that we would fully fund the defence investment plan. I’ve spent a lot of time on that and it will be fully funded.

There was a shortfall - there won’t be [at the budget].

Andy Burnham has suggested that it would not be legitimate for a party to form a majority government with less than 30% of the vote.

In his Today interview, asked why he wanted electoral reform and a move towards proportional representation, Burnham replied:

double quotation markI found it better being elected under a different system as mayor of Greater Manchester, where people had one or two, they could put that on the ballot paper.

Because you had a reason to stop on every doorstep and chat to people who might not always support your party and try and get their second preference.

And I also feel that in an era of five party politics, can we really watch a party with less than 30% just walk into Downing Street? Is that something we should feel comfortable about?

As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham was elected under the supplementary vote system. This means, if no candidate gets more than 50% when the votes are counted, the top two go into a run-off and then second preferences are taken into account.

When it was put to Burnham that he was just saying that because he wanted to stop Nigel Farage becoming prime minister, Burnham replied:

double quotation markNo, it could happen with any political party. It’s whether that would be a legitimate government.

In the 20th century, when two-party politics was the norm, parties that went on to form a government normally had at least 40% of the national vote – and sometimes a lot more.

But, with the revival of the Liberals, and then the Lib Dems, the success of nationalist parties in Scotland and Wales, and now the emergence of the Greens and Reform UK as significant parties, it would now be quite possible for a party to win a Westminster majority with under 30% of the vote.

At the last election, Labour won a landslide victory with just 33.7% of the vote.

Andy Burnham has said that it is “completely wrong” to claim that he is picking on pensioners with the plans he announced yesterday.

When this claim was put to him in an interview on ITV’s Good Morning Britain, Burnham replied:

double quotation markI think you’ve got it completely wrong really, if you don’t mind me saying, to put it like that, because I have put out … a vision for a national care service.

There are pensioners out there who watch your programme who are paying for care costs from their basic state pension. Now, is that right or fair?

We have to fix this system. But what I’m saying about the triple lock enables a better support, better care for people in their homes. No care charges.

So, please let me just make that point that people need to see these things in the round. It’s a better deal for older people going forward.

Household energy bills in Great Britain are predicted to soar by £276 a year for the typical household from January as the impact of the Middle East war continues through the coldest months of winter, Jillian Ambrose reports.

In his Today interview, Andy Burnham also said that he thought Britain needed to resolve what its relationship with the EU should be because it could not afford another decade of drift.

double quotation markWhat I am saying is it’s not good enough to leave that question just hanging.

I am saying, let’s be clear about where we want Britain to go in the next decade. And I’ve asked people to join with me on that.

The country cannot have a decade, another one like the one we’ve just had, where we’ve had too much drift, too much division.

I am very clear, and I will say this bluntly, Brexit has caused more harm than good and I think around 60% of the British public agree with that statement.

So the question is what do we do about that?

And I’m not doing the usual politician thing. I’m being honest about facing up to that, and give people options that they can look at and judge.

Here is more detail on what Andy Burnham said about the possibility of rejoining the EU when he was being interviewed by Nick Robinson on the Today programme.

When Robinson put it to Burnham that ideally he wanted to rejoin, Burnham paused before saying: “I want to look at the options.”

Robinson said that was a long pause, and it sounded as if he meant yes, but did not want to say so.

double quotation markI have said it, there’s no point me denying it, I’ve said in the book I would like to see Britain rejoin in my lifetime. So there was no point saying otherwise.

But it’s not necessarily the case that is now. Because we need to understand what would be the nature of how we would look at the different options.

Burnham then set out four options; the status quo, joining a customs union, joining a customs union and the single market, or rejoining. (See 7.49am.)

Burnham seemed to be referring to his book, Head North, which he co-wrote with Steve Rotheram. In that, they set out an extensive plan for political reform. But they did not say much in it about Brexit.

However, Burnham did declare last year that he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU in his lifetime.

Andy Burnham has said that it is not accurate to say that he is getting rid of the pensions triple lock.

In interviews this morning, he challenged this description because the plan he announced yesterday means that the value of the state pension will continue to rise in line with prices, earnings or 2.5%.

But under the current system, pensions rise every year either by 2.5%, or by inflation, or by the annual rise in earnings – which is highest.

After 2030, normally they will rise by 2.5% or by inflation. But if that is not enough to ensure that pensions have risen in line with the average increase in earnings since the policy was introduced, they will rise by that amount.

The pensions triple lock is not a benefit; it is an uprating mechanism, and what Burnham announced means that the earnings element of that mechanism will apply according to a new formula.

The change will save money because, under the current system, if the rise in earnings is particularly big one year, as sometimes happens, there is a rachet effect, and the increase gets baked in for future years.

double quotation markThe decision on the triple lock, the adjustment – and it is an adjustment – it’s not getting rid of the whole concept of the triple lock.

Andy Burnham has said that the government does not have “huge room for manoeuvre” as it looks at how it can help people with the cost of living.

In his interview with BBC Breakfast, Burnham said:

double quotation markWe’re thinking all of the time, ‘how do we take a bit of pressure off people, give them some breathing space?’

It’s why one of the first decisions I took as prime minister was to remove VAT off electricity bills, and that will happen on Thursday …

We’ll do something to help people with bus fares next year, the £2 cap for the whole of the year, and then in the budget we will consider further measures.

It’s important for me to say that we don’t have huge room for manoeuvre.

I think people can see that when they look at the financial picture, but within that we will do our best, and we’ll also try to support people who are struggling with the cost of doing business ’cause it’s hard to run a business right now as well.

Andy Burnham has said that he accepts there will could be an energy crisis this winter.

In his interview with the Today programme, Burnham was asked if he agreed with Simone Rossi, CEO of the energy company EDF, who told the programme in an interview that Britain was “walking into a second significant energy crisis after the one we experienced just four years ago”.

double quotation markI don’t think that is an overstatement to be honest.

The situation was “very challenging” for people buying petrol, or heating their homes, he said.

double quotation markI’m doing what I can, removing say VAT off bills. But it is very difficult indeed, and it’s why the Middle East situation needs to command a lot of our attention.

Asked what he might be able to do to help people, Burnham told BBC Breakfast:

double quotation markI’m considering everything that might help people in very difficult times and I will be honest and say every possible measure is being looked at.

The question I’ve got is, how many can I afford, what can we do given the state of the public finances?

And people wouldn’t thank me for making unfunded payments that then cause pressure on mortgages – and we’ve seen that in the past and we’re not going back there.

Burnham said, when he talked about considering every possible measure to help with energy costs, that included looking at whether to scrap a fuel duty increase planned for next year.

Good morning. Andy Burnham’s speech is getting a mixed review in the papers, but there is general consensus that it is a consequential one – not one that we will have forgotten within a fortnight or so, but one that will make the next list of all-time important Labour conference speeches of the last 50 years.

If you are still catching up, here are three good places to start.

Pippa Crerar’s overnight splash for the Guardian.

The conference wraps up today, with four cabinet ministers speaking. But much of the attention will be on digesting the significance of what the PM said yesterday.

Burnham has given a series of interviews which are playing out this morning. Speaking to the Today programme, Burnham confirmed that, when he told delegates yesterday he would be looking at ways of having a better relationship with the EU, rejoining would be one of the options.

double quotation markWe could stay as we are. That’s definitely an option, if people think this is the right place to stay.

We could look at what [former Conservative chancellor] George Osborne has said about a customs union, we could look at what the Liberal Democrats said at their conference about the single market or we could go all the way.

There are clearly options that need to be considered, and we have to look at what is doable and what would be the pros and cons of each.

I will post more from his interviews soon.

9.45am: Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, speaks.

10.15am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, speaks.

11.10am: Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, speaks.

12.10pm: Lucy Powell, the deputy leader, gives the final speech of the conference.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: SEN RAND PAUL: Our budget deficit is out of control. Congress must pass my Six Penny Plan
articles.excerpt:
GOP Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky told Fox News Digital that he does not support the prospect of distributing "dividends when there's a deficit."

In 2011, our national debt was about $15 trillion, and t...
articles.body_text:
GOP Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky told Fox News Digital that he does not support the prospect of distributing "dividends when there's a deficit."

In 2011, our national debt was about $15 trillion, and the U.S. Treasury spent over $450 billion on interest. Washington was printing money it didn’t have, buying its way out of yet another financial crisis and sending brand-new, taxpayer-funded subsidies to health insurance companies through Obamacare. It was clear then that this massive level of spending was not sustainable.

It was in this moment of explosive deficit spending that a new generation of conservative leaders—myself included—rode into Congress on a mandate from the American people to restore fiscal sanity and financial freedom. I left my medical practice to stand for public office because I would not let our children and grandchildren be bankrupted by reckless politicians.

The fight for fiscal responsibility continues, and I plan to force a vote on my latest balanced budget proposal—the Six Penny Plan—later this year.

GOP FISCAL HAWK SOUNDS ALARM ON 'OUT OF CONTROL' FEDERAL SPENDING, SAYING 'BOTH PARTIES HAVE FAILED US'

But I regret to inform you that Congress has completely lost the plot.

Under the Six Penny Plan, Congress needs to find a six-percentage-point cut each year for five years. After that, once the budget is balanced, spending can increase based on the additional revenue from economic growth.

The national debt has now surpassed $40 trillion. Congress now spends over $1 trillion on interest every year. Congress spends more on interest than on national defense. This enormous debt is contributing to rising interest rates and inflation, hurting every American. It’s a blinking red warning light—just as bright and red as the ink on our budget documents.

Congress’ answer to this growing fiscal bomb? More of the same. Congress passed a continuing resolution earlier this summer to extend the status quo and will debate another extension before the end of this year.

It doesn’t have to be this way. When Congress takes up government funding later this year, it can pass my Six Penny Plan, which will balance the budget within five years. (Douglas Rissing)

The good news is that it doesn’t have to be this way. When Congress takes up government funding later this year, it can pass my Six Penny Plan, which will balance the budget within five years.

$50 TRILLION IN DEBT IS NOT A DISTANT THREAT. AMERICA IS SPEEDING TOWARDS IT

No one can say he or she supports a balanced budget while voting against the only balanced budget that came up for a vote. No more empty promises. No more excuses. No more games.

The Six Penny Plan doesn’t prescribe any particular program or budget category to be cut—it even specifically exempts Social Security from cuts. The Six Penny Plan simply sets a maximum spending level. What Congress wants to do within that maximum is up for debate. This budget reflects the basic questions of priorities many Americans have confronted at different points in their lives, whether because of unexpected expenses or a loss of income: Which expenses can Congress keep, and which can Congress cut? Under the Six Penny Plan, Congress needs to find a six percent cut each year for five years. After that, once the budget is balanced, spending can increase based on the additional revenue from economic growth.

WASHINGTON IS DRIVING AMERICA TOWARD A DEBT CRISIS WE CAN'T IGNORE ANY LONGER

Interestingly, when I first proposed what became the Penny Plan in 2018, Congress would not have had to find any cuts, but merely work within a spending freeze for five years. Its inaction then is only making the job harder now.

In subsequent years, it became the Penny Plan when it required a one percent cut, then it became the "Pennies Plan," and today it is the Six Penny Plan because it requires us to find six pennies out of every dollar.

CONGRESS SPENDS $7 TRILLION. HERE’S HOW THAT MATH WORKS OUT IF YOU THINK OF JUST $100

Kicking the can down the road has been standard procedure in Congress for too long. Lawmakers have treated the debt like someone else’s problem, to be dealt with some other day in the future. Well, the future has arrived. Every year that Congress does nothing only adds fuel to the debt bomb and increases the risk of a bigger explosion down the road.

It’s also time to call inaction on the debt what it is: a vote to increase the hidden inflation tax on everyone; a willful decision to let inflation wreak havoc on our cost of living. Inaction is unacceptable.

The Six Penny Plan is the answer. The good news is that, when it was voted on in 2024 and 2025, the Six Penny Plan was supported by a majority of Senate Republicans. Because a budget resolution needs only a majority vote to pass, rather than a supermajority, Senate Republicans have the numbers to pass the Six Penny Plan.

In other words, this is the moment. Support for the Six Penny Plan has been building, and there should be enough votes. Let’s show that conservatives mean what we say and can follow through on our promises to balance the budget.

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM SEN RAND PAUL

Republican Rand Paul represents Kentucky in the United States Senate. He is the author of "The Case Against Socialism" (Broadside Books, October 15, 2019).

Theo Francken says bloc is in a ‘difficult position’ after recent increase in hybrid provocations from Moscow

Belgian defence minister Theo Francken said “there will be more hybrid threat actions” in the coming months, as he starkly warned “it will be a dark winter for Europe.”

Speaking at Euronews’s Defence and Space Summit, Francken said hybrid warfare “is not something that Russia [has been] doing for two or three years,” but for much longer and it has “expertise” in this area, often making it difficult for western countries to investigate them and attribute responsibility.

He particularly worried about Russia’s increased use of jet-powered drones.

“We need to scale up ⁠our air defences and ​we ​need to ​have more stocks, ​scale ‌up production. ​Everything ​has to go faster,” he said.

He said Belgium used to be “the worse pupil in class” two years ago with low defence spending, but it has since improved and ramped it up its planning.

He said Europe got too used to its comfortable welfare state protections at the cost of adequate spending on defence, and this is now changing.

“Europe has been very good in investing in soft power, in social security. And it’s beautiful to have a pension system, to have social welfare systems [for] when somebody gets sick, when somebody lost his job – we have everything. But when there’s war or there’s hybrid threats, we don’t have anything. So yeah, we’re in a really difficult position.”

Russia has ⁠moved to mass ⁠attacks ⁠on Ukraine’s energy ​infrastructure, Ukrainian prime ⁠minister Sergii Koretskyi said, after ​overnight ‌strikes ‌on energy facilities in ‌the capital and other regions, Reuters reported.

Debris ⁠had been found ⁠at ⁠the premises ​of one of ⁠the western embassies ⁠in ​the ‌centre ‌of Ukraine’s capital, ‌Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said this morning, citing preliminary ‌information.

Klitschko did not ​name the embassy, ⁠but said ​emergency services were ​heading ​to the ​site.

It comes after another night of Russian drone attacks on Ukraine, which damaged energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure.

Russia said it targeted a communications centre and energy facilities in Kyiv, and port infrastructure in Izmail, among others.

Neighbouring Poland issued a high readiness emergency alert to residents of south-eastern part of the country this morning, as it scrambled military aircraft to monitor the situation.

articles.title: Greggs to close four UK factories with potential for 740 job losses
articles.excerpt:
Bakery chain says move is necessary to provide growth in the ‘most cost-efficient manner’

Greggs has announced plans to close four of its factories, in a move that could result in 740 job losses over...
articles.body_text:
Bakery chain says move is necessary to provide growth in the ‘most cost-efficient manner’

Greggs has announced plans to close four of its factories, in a move that could result in 740 job losses over the next two and a half years.

The bakery chain said it was consulting on the closures, which would initially cost £60m when including disruption costs and redundancy payments, but then could create £20m of savings each year by 2028.

The proposed cuts come as Greggs reported stronger sales growth in its most recent quarter at 7.7%, up from 7.2% in the first half of the year. The company said the closures, “whilst difficult, are necessary” to ensure it can grow in the “most cost-efficient manner”.

“Our immediate priority is to minimise the impact on our people where possible,” it said. “We will enter into a consultation period shortly to work with trade unions and employee representatives of those affected to refine and develop these proposals.”

The closures could affect factories in Enfield, north London, Penrith in Cumbria, Kelso in Roxburghshire, Scotland, and Seaham in County Durham. It will continue to run distribution operations from Enfield. The proposals could also affect manufacturing operations at its Treforest site in Wales, but this will continue as a distribution centre for business.

Greggs has grown to become Britain’s biggest fast food business thanks to the popularity of its low-cost pastries, cakes and hot drinks. It has expanded rapidly this year, with 57 net new openings, as part of its plan to open between 100 and 110 shops by the end of 2026.

Iced matcha lattes and a bigger range of salads and chicken rolls also helped to boost sales over the summer, the company said. However, Greggs told investors on Wednesday that while stronger sales had “modestly improved” its outlook for this year, “there are signs of greater inflationary pressures in 2027”.

Alex Pugh, an analyst at the investment broker Freetrade, said that while the bakery chain “has survived a heatwave and a cost-of-living crisis … a £1.50 sausage roll could be a real test of loyalty”.

Earlier this year, the company raised the cost of its bestseller sausage roll by 5p, taking it to £1.35 in most shops. It also increased the price of a latte by 10p, taking it to £2.25, as it looked for ways to combat rising wage, energy and packaging costs.

Shares in Greggs rose by 7.3% in early trading on Wednesday morning, making it the best performer across the mid-cap FTSE 250 index and taking its year to date rise to 17%. Greggs, which is headquartered in Newcastle, employs more than 33,000 people around the UK.

articles.title: 'He will never walk free': Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
articles.excerpt:
More than 69,000 cases of child sexual abuse were recorded in India in 2024 alone (representative image)

An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring ...
articles.body_text:
More than 69,000 cases of child sexual abuse were recorded in India in 2024 alone (representative image)

An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.

Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".

The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).

At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage".

"When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor.

"Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.

Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth".

"The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again.

"The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."

Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".

Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.

It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.

Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.

Tensions in Indian state after 11-year-old raped and murdered

The child abuse survivor fighting to save others

India media storm over 10-year-old pregnant rape victim

The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.

Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.

The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data, external.

And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.

Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.

In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.

After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

articles.title: Africa's richest man to launch Kenya oil refinery despite land protests
articles.excerpt:
Aliko Dangote made his fortune in cement before branching into oil

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lam...
articles.body_text:
Aliko Dangote made his fortune in cement before branching into oil

Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote and Kenya's President William Ruto are set to break ground on a $16bn (£12bn) oil refinery in Lamu, on Kenya's northern coast.

Upon completion, the refinery is expected to process 700,000 barrels of crude oil a day, making it East Africa's largest industrial project by capacity.

Ahead of the launch, some local residents took to the streets to demand more compensation for land used for the refinery.

Speaking to the BBC, Dangote dismissed the protests as games played by local marketers and international players, insisting the refinery would go ahead and would be ready by 2030 as planned.

The Lamu refinery is Kenya's largest infrastructure project since independence, surpassing the $5.1bn (£3.9bn) Standard Gauge Railway. East Africa does not currently have any oil refineries.

In his interview with the BBC's Focus on Africa programme, Dangote disputed the compensation claims and said the company took only the portion of land it needed from what the government made available.

"To come and say some people are demonstrating, demonstrating about what? Have you ever seen people demonstrating against themselves in terms of development?" he asked, indicating he was not fazed by the protests.

At the height of construction, Dangote, who is Africa's richest man, said the refinery would create 60,000 jobs, with the benefits extending beyond those employed directly by the project.

"Are we going to bring robots? Of course, the people will benefit," he said.

Critics have questioned the decision to build the refinery in Kenya, which is not an oil-producing country. Others have suggested Tanzania or Uganda, both of which are moving towards oil exports through the East African Crude Oil Pipeline.

But Kenya's Energy and Petroleum Minister Opiyo Wandayi told the BBC that the refinery's location did not mean it would rely on oil from the region.

"Refineries get crude oil from the market. And the market is open," he said.

Dangote made a similar point, citing Singapore as an example.

"Singapore doesn't produce a single drop of oil, yet they have a lot of refineries," Dangote said.

Dangote speaks to the BBC about his new oil refinery in Kenya

The refinery will also include a 1,000-megawatt power plant.

Dangote sees reliable electricity as a critical constraint on industrialisation across Africa, particularly in mineral-rich countries that still export raw materials rather than processing them locally.

He has about $50bn (£38bn) worth of projects in the pipeline, including plans to develop 10,000 megawatts of power generation capacity across Africa by 2030, with the potential to double that depending on demand.

In Lamu, the new power plant is designed to support Dangote's operations as well as other industries expected to set up in the area.

"The power is there and what you do is what we call plug and play," he said.

Kenya has relatively high fuel prices, raising expectations that greater refining capacity could eventually help bring down pump prices. However, the price of crude oil, the main raw material for fuel, set by international markets, remains a major factor in what consumers pay at the pump.

The Lamu refinery is Dangote's largest proposed investment outside Nigeria, with construction due to begin on 1 November. His refinery in Nigeria also has a processing capacity of 700,000 barrels a day.

Dangote plans to double that capacity after floating 4.1 million ordinary shares to raise up to $2.1b earlier this month.
