articles.title: S Korea demands apology over DMZ blasts as N Korea denies planting mines
articles.excerpt:
South Korea’s military has demanded an apology from North Korea over landmine explosions earlier this month in the border zone between the two countries that wounded three soldiers.

Three South Korea...
articles.body_text:
South Korea’s military has demanded an apology from North Korea over landmine explosions earlier this month in the border zone between the two countries that wounded three soldiers.

Three South Korean soldiers were injured in two explosions on September 21 near the military demarcation line in the western section of the Demilitarized Zone, a heavily fortified border buffer zone between the Koreas that is commonly known as the DMZ.

Kang Hyunwoo, the South Korean joint chiefs of staff’s director of operations, said the military “strongly urges” North Korea to apologise for the blasts and take “responsible measures” to prevent a recurrence.

“This is a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements; it must be stopped immediately,” he said on Wednesday, adding “we strongly urge an apology and responsible measures”.

Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul said South Korea would consider unspecified “corresponding measures” if a complete investigation confirms the North was responsible.

Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the South Korean assessment is a “conspiratorial farce” and accused Seoul of making groundless claims to create a pretext for provocation against Pyongyang.

She also criticised the South for broadcasting warnings and firing warning shots at North Korean troops conducting front-line fortification work, adding “our soldiers have never crossed the border”.

“If the [South Korean] military gangsters fire at our soldiers carrying on the permanent project for the southern border, not warning shots, our border units will take immediate and merciless retaliatory action,” she said.

The United Nations Command said on Wednesday it had “identified an active Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea’s) anti-personnel mine on the ROK side of the Military Demarcation Line”, in a joint investigation with Seoul’s military.

“Based on the findings of the investigation, UNC determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred,” it added.

The UN Command is a US-led multinational military force charged with overseeing the armistice agreement that halted fighting in the Korean War and administers the southern side of the DMZ.

articles.title: Flydubai flight to Israel diverted to Saudi Arabia after emergency alert
articles.excerpt:
A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The Flydubai plane transmitted an emergency alert shortly ...
articles.body_text:
A commercial plane travelling from Dubai in the United Arab Emirates to Israel has been forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

The Flydubai plane transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information.

The airline confirmed that the plane “experienced an incident while en route”, adding that it landed safely at Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk airport and all passengers are safe and accounted for.

It said more details will be shared later.

The incident that caused the plane to issue an “unlawful interference” alert was apparently due to an altercation between the pilots on board the flight, Israeli media outlets reported, quoting Israeli officials.

The Israeli military said in a statement that Israeli Chief of the General Staff Eyal Zamir held an assessment of the incident with senior officers after the reported incident.

articles.title: Poundland management in rescue talks that could save 11,000 jobs
articles.excerpt:
Ex-Asda boss Andy Bond linked to plan, with buyout team understood to be negotiating with financial backer

Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a rescue bid for the ailing cut-...
articles.body_text:
Ex-Asda boss Andy Bond linked to plan, with buyout team understood to be negotiating with financial backer

Poundland’s management team are in “advanced talks” to lead a rescue bid for the ailing cut-price retailer that could save up to 11,000 jobs.

The former Asda boss Andy Bond, who ran Poundland for a number of years from 2016 then stepped up to its former parent Pepco before leaving in 2025, is understood to be part of the negotiations to take on the business.

The management buyout team, which includes the current boss, Barry Williams, is understood to be negotiating with an unnamed financial backer.

Poundland’s current owners, Gordon Brothers, last month hired the advisory company Alvarez & Marsal to oversee a sale of the business at a reported price of £30m. The process has fuelled fears that the restructuring specialist is set on breaking up the retailer despite improved trading.

Interested parties are thought to include the US company Fortress, which owns Poundstretcher, and Modella Capital, the UK-based private equity owner of Hobbycraft and TG Jones that this year put the UK arm of Claire’s and The Original Factory Shop into administration. Neither of these players are involved with Bond’s team.

Sources said these financial companies were among those placing a first round of bids at the start of this week that are to be considered as early as Wednesday.

One source said very few bids were expected to include the entire business and it was a “great shame” if an offer to keep the business trading was not considered.

The discount chain, which employs 11,000 people and has 600 stores, said last week that it had returned to growth of 3.3% at established stores in the latest three-month period. “Profitability is on a strongly improving trajectory with expected pre-tax earnings around £80m better than last year.”

The company registered an £85m pre-tax loss in the year to the end of September 2025 but said it had a cash pile of more than £30m and several sources of borrowings.

Gordon Brothers had put in place a £95m lending facility, of which only £50m had been used, Poundland said.

The restructuring specialist, which bought Poundland from for £1 from Pepco Group in June 2025, agreed to pump £80m into the company as part of a rescue deal last year.

About 149 Poundland stores shut with the loss of 2,200 jobs under the rescue shake-up launched after challenging trading conditions and unpopular clothing ranges sent the retailer into the red.

It has since refocused on £1 items and relaunched its Pep & Co clothing brand after a switch to ranges supplied by its former parent group hit sales

However, the uncertainty about Poundland’s future has reportedly prompted an insurer to some of Poundland’s suppliers to pull credit. The move could cause problems with its supply of goods.

articles.title: South Korea calls for apology from North Korea after mine injures three soldiers
articles.excerpt:
Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels

South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured ...
articles.body_text:
Blast during search operation near border fuels political tensions amid attempts to revive diplomatic channels

South Korea has demanded an apology from North Korea over a landmine blast that injured three soldiers, saying they were hurt by North Korean mines on the southern side of the border.

Kang Hyun-woo, the director of operations at South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff, demanded an apology and “responsible measures” from Pyongyang over the blast, which occurred on 21 September during a search operation south of the border.

He also called for an immediate halt to North Korea’s mine-laying and border fortification, which he said violated the armistice and the spirit of inter-Korean agreements. North Korea would bear “all responsibility” for any future developments, he said.

The incident echoes a 2015 mine blast in the demilitarised zone between the countries that seriously injured two South Korean soldiers and prompted Seoul to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers. North Korea responded to the move with artillery fire across the border before expressing regret during high-level talks.

The US-led UN command (UNC), which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, said on Wednesday that a joint investigation with South Korea’s military had identified a live North Korean anti-personnel mine on the southern side of the military demarcation line (MDL), the de facto border.

The UNC said an armistice violation had occurred and that it was addressing the issue through “established armistice mechanisms”.

The explosions occurred about 10 metres south of the MDL on the western front, as troops searched an area where North Korea was suspected of laying mines.

Two blasts went off about a minute apart, seriously injuring a battalion commander, whose foot was reportedly severed at the ankle, and an engineer. A third officer was present and has minor injuries from the explosion.

On Monday, South Korea’s military said interim findings showed the blasts were “highly likely” to have been caused by North Korean mines

North Korea has denied involvement. In a statement carried by state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the sister of leader Kim Jong-un, called the incident “an obvious self-staged farce”.

“Our soldiers have never once crossed the border,” she said, warning that if South Korean troops fired directly at North Korean soldiers, border units would carry out “immediate and merciless retaliation”.

Chris Green, a senior consultant at the International Crisis Group, said the investigation findings would not settle the matter politically because the North would always have “guaranteed plausible deniability”.

There are no working communication channels between the two Koreas. Pyongyang severed ties in 2024, declared South Korea a hostile state and has since laid mines and built fortifications along the border. “Accidental escalation on the Korean peninsula is always just a few steps away and it’s fewer steps now than it was in 2015,” Green said.

The blast presents a challenge for South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, who has sought to revive diplomacy with Pyongyang. Last week, he told the UN general assembly that Seoul would be a “pacemaker” for peace, and urged Washington to ease sanctions in exchange for a freeze on North Korea’s weapons programmes.

The incident has also fuelled political tensions at home. Opposition politicians questioned whether the investigation had been delayed to avoid overshadowing Lee’s UN speech, a suggestion the presidential office denied.

The conservative People Power party has also called for the return of the propaganda loudspeakers, which were switched off and dismantled under Lee last year.

The mine blast adds to other diplomatic difficulties facing Lee. On Monday, Seoul demanded an apology from Ukraine after its president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, disclosed the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the transfer secret, citing the men’s safety and diplomatic and security considerations. Some critics said the secrecy was about not upsetting Pyongyang.

articles.title: ‘If people are in a bunker, business stops’: Missile alerts cost Ukraine $45m for every hour they halt businesses
articles.excerpt:
Minister tells Guardian of trade-offs Kyiv facing as it tries to keep normal life moving amid Russian strikes

Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring bus...
articles.body_text:
Minister tells Guardian of trade-offs Kyiv facing as it tries to keep normal life moving amid Russian strikes

Missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, according to the country’s economy minister, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment.

Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to “destroy pretty much the entire economy”.

“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks.

Speaking from the heavily protected government building in Kyiv, Kravchenko, a former McKinsey executive who joined the government in the summer, said the attacks were forcing large parts of the economy into repeated standstills as workers were sent to shelters, with sirens lasting up to 10 hours a day.

“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” he said.

To ease the economic costs, the government recently introduced a new two-tier warning system designed to keep businesses operating during prolonged air raid alerts.

A “red” alert warns of a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning is used for drone threats, allowing many businesses to remain open.

More than half of businesses were continuing to operate during yellow alerts, Kravchenko said.

But a yellow alert is no guarantee of safety. That danger was made clear on Monday, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people while staff were still inside working.

It is one of the difficult trade-offs Ukraine faces as it tries to keep normal life moving while protecting people from an escalating campaign of Russian strikes.

Kravchenko said Russian attacks this year alone had caused an estimated $10bn in damage to fixed assets, with steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, most recently datacentres, among the targets. Russia has also effectively blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, which before the blockade carried the bulk of the country’s exports.

The minister believed the government was better prepared this year for what could be the “hardest, the harshest winter” of the war, with further pressure expected on energy supplies, infrastructure and businesses already weakened by months of strikes.

To protect against future strikes, the government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukraine’s air-defence system, the minister said, although he cautioned that businesses could never fully protect themselves from Russian missiles and drones.

The ongoing damage from strikes has added to an already severe strain on the state’s finances.

The president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged, despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027.

Kravchenko said the government had since narrowed the shortfall to $20bn through spending cuts and by identifying additional domestic reserves.

Kyiv was now seeking further support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potentially bringing forward loans that had been earmarked for next year, Kravchenko said.

“There is very active work with all our international partners to get additional sources of funding,” he said.

Kravchenko dismissed suggestions that the shortfall was the result of mismanagement or corruption. He also said it was not due to excessive spending under former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whose drive to overhaul military procurement and rapidly expand Ukraine’s drone programme had made him one of the government’s most prominent reformers before his dismissal in July, a move that triggered street protests.

Instead, he said the gap reflected both weaker-than-expected state revenues and the rising cost of waging the war.

“The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said, pointing to the need for more air-defence systems and for Ukraine to accelerate development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered weapons.

But high-profile corruption scandals have also reached Zelenskyy’s inner circle, straining trust in the government both at home and among western donors.

A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that corruption in government was the most cited concern among Ukrainians, named by 50% of respondents, ahead of mass missile and drone strikes at 40%. The same survey found that 72% believed Zelenskyy bore personal responsibility for corrupt actions by people around him.

Kravchenko said progress had been made to tackle the issue but admitted that Ukraine faced both corruption itself and a persistent perception problem both inside Ukraine and abroad.

“I very much appreciate the pressure of European partners on reforms,” he said, adding that Ukraine also needed to tackle perceptions of corruption at home and abroad.

Ukraine’s external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6bn, but only about $20bn has so far been secured, according to the minister, with further tax rises and spending cuts under discussion.

Asked whether the rise of parties sceptical of support for Ukraine in France and Germany could weaken western commitment to Kyiv, he said: “Am I worried? I think I should be, probably.”

“The overall fatigue is increasing in Europe,” he added.

articles.title: Repeat offender with lengthy rap sheet accused of gunning down Kentucky trooper during traffic stop
articles.excerpt:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Tennessee man accused of killing a Kentucky state trooper was on probation and already wanted for a violation, wit...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Tennessee man accused of killing a Kentucky state trooper was on probation and already wanted for a violation, with a criminal record that included assault, fraud and illegally possessing a gun.

Emonnie Branch, 51, was denied bond Tuesday on a charge of murder of a first responder in the death of Trooper Hayden Phillips, a husband and father of three young boys.

Tennessee Department of Correction records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Branch was serving five years of probation for a fraud-related conviction. His supervision was scheduled to end in July 2030.

Sumner County District Attorney Thomas Dean told Fox 17 Nashville that Branch was already wanted for a probation violation tied to his securities fraud conviction before Monday’s shooting.

CALIFORNIA GUNMAN REPEATEDLY RELEASED BEFORE DEADLY RAMPAGE, FIERY SHOOTOUT WITH DEPUTIES

Emonnie Branch, 51, is being held without bond in the killing of Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips. (Warren County Detention Center)

"Looks like he has a very extensive and varied criminal history," Commonwealth’s Attorney Kori Bumgarner said during Tuesday’s arraignment, the outlet reported.

CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND

Emonnie Branch was on probation when he was accused of killing Trooper Hayden Phillips, Tennessee correction records show. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

Dean said Branch’s prior convictions included attempted domestic assault, violating a no-contact order and securities fraud. Court records reviewed by the outlet also showed a 2009 conviction for illegally possessing a firearm as a convicted felon.

Fox 17 reported that Branch was arrested twice this year for probation violations. Warren County Regional Jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital show he is being held without bond on the murder charge and a fugitive charge.

SUSPECTS AT LARGE AFTER TUCSON POLICE RECRUIT KILLED, PIMA COUNTY CORRECTIONS OFFICER WOUNDED IN SHOOTING

Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips was killed while patrolling Interstate 65 in Warren County on Monday. (KY State Police)

Phillips was shot and killed during a traffic stop on Interstate 65 in Warren County Monday, Kentucky State Police said. Authorities identified Branch as the suspect and issued a statewide Blue Alert before Louisville Metro Police captured him that evening.

"He was senselessly murdered," U.S. Attorney Kyle Bumgarner said Monday night during a news briefing. "We have a wife that expected her husband to come home. We have three little boys who don’t have a dad."

JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER

Kentucky State Police released an image of a Honda Civic they said was present during the shooting of Trooper Hayden Phillips on Interstate 65. (KY State Police)

"One of our own was gunned down and murdered on the side of the road," Kyle Bumgarner added.

He pledged that the Justice Department would give state prosecutors and investigators "every tool" and "every bit of support" it could to help them pursue the maximum sentence.

Kentucky State Police Commissioner Col. Phillip Burnett Jr. condemned the suspect’s "cowardly actions" and explained why he had mentioned his name only once.

"I want you to know I only mentioned his name one time," Burnett said.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND

"We will seek justice for Hayden," he continued. "Let me repeat that, we will seek justice for Hayden. We will not rest until this happens."

Phillips was a three-year state police veteran assigned to Post 3 in Bowling Green. Burnett promised his family the agency would stand beside them.

"You will not walk this path alone," he said.

Phillips’ wife, Jordan, shared her grief Tuesday.

DRUNK WRONG-WAY DRIVER KILLED MASS TROOPER AFTER 9 DRINKS AT BAR, DA REPORT SAYS

Flowers and stuffed animals surround a cruiser outside Kentucky State Police Post 3 in tribute to fallen Trooper Hayden Phillips. (Governor Andy Beshear)

"I’ve laid here all night waiting for him to come home… for the radio to click off, the gun belt to hang," she wrote on Facebook.

"I promise to pick up all the pieces and force myself to carry on for your boys. I know you would want me to," she added.

State police escorted Phillips’ body to Glasgow Tuesday. A candlelight vigil is scheduled for Thursday at 6:30 p.m. local time.

Gov. Andy Beshear ordered flags at all state buildings lowered to half-staff from sunrise to sunset Sunday, Oct. 4, in honor of Phillips.

"Trooper Hayden Phillips was a hero who sacrificed everything protecting our people and our commonwealth, and it is our sacred duty to honor him and his family," Beshear said.

He urged Kentuckians to pray for Jordan and their three children and encouraged donations to the Kentucky State Police Foundation, saying all proceeds would go directly to the family.

Jordan asked people to share memories of her husband with their sons.

"He was just the kind of guy who is easy to celebrate," she wrote.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

David Shoebridge has been named the new federal leader of the Greens, with Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy, Guardian Australia understands.

The Greens will make a formal announcement in Sydney shortly.

The party’s ten senators and lone MP met to decide the new leadership team during a pre-planned two day retreat in Sydney, and followed the shock resignation of Larissa Waters on Monday, due to ill health.

The leadership became a three-way race after Shoebridge announced his run on Wednesday morning. The South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young had declared her candidacy on Tuesday, followed by a joint ticket of NSW senator and former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi and treasury spokesperson senator Nick McKim.

Shoebridge entered federal parliament in 2022, after more than a decade in NSW state politics. He holds the Greens’ defence and foreign affairs portfolios, and is a forceful presence in parliamentary debates, on social media and in Senate estimates hearings.

Before politics, he was a corporate lawyer and then became a barrister specialising in employment law, and at one point was a Labor branch member in Sydney’s inner west. In the early 2000s he met the hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon, who went on to become his mentor.

Hodgins-May is one of the Greens’ newest members, and entered parliament in May 2024, filling a casual vacancy created by Janet Rice’s retirement.

Under Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and more recently supported Labor’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The Greens also teamed up with the Coalition and crossbench in the Senate to force Labor to drop a controversial $5000 cap for veterans to access allied health services, and compelled the government to bring forward 20,000 aged care beds.

In a statement released ahead of the leadership ballot, Shoebridge and Hodgins-May said they were “excited by what we can and must do together as Greens.”

“This is the time to build our movement as the home for every Australia who wants action on the climate crisis, a fair return from our resources, a secure home and income, and not to sell out our independence to the US or the 1%.

“We do not seek to reform Labor, but to replace them.

“The answer to the rise of One Nation and the far right is giving people hope, and making people’s lives better with real economic and environmental security. It is as simple as a meal before school, as clear as no new coal and gas, and as challenging as holding back the wave of US billionaire tech bros and their vampire AI data centres.”

Waters revealed she would quit to focus on treatment for kidney disease, after her health had declined significantly since being elected leader in May last year. She is expected to take medical leave before returning to the Senate.

The party’s new leader will come under pressure to bring a more forceful approach to the job, amid frustrations with Waters’ more moderate style, and the party’s inability to exploit growing moves by voters away from Labor and the Coalition.

The former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather on Tuesday called for the party’s membership to get a vote in the leadership race.

articles.title: Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years
articles.excerpt:
Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history

After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal over...
articles.body_text:
Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history

After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal oversight, marking the end of the longest arrangement of this kind in US history.

In the early 2000s, a group of police officers known as the “riders” were exposed for offenses like planting evidence, falsifying reports and using excessive force against primarily young Black men. These actions led victims to file more than 100 civil lawsuits against the department. In 2003, as a part of the settlement of these cases, OPD was put on a federal court-ordered reform program.

OPD was given more than 50 tasks to complete including collecting and analyzing data on racial profiling, dealing with complaints against officers more quickly and updating their community policing practices. Despite this, issues remained and the department’s reforms were put under the direct control of a federal judge in 2012.

Since then, the department has still had its share of scandals including allegations that several OPD officers sex-trafficked a teenage girl; nearly a dozen officers were either fired or suspended. The investigation into the trafficking of the teenager began in 2015 and OPD issued her a nearly $1m settlement in 2017.

For organizers against police misconduct and brutality, the decision to end the federal oversight scheme does not mean that the department should be free of scrutiny.

“Police cannot police themselves. Oakland’s history has already taught us that lesson,” the Anti Police-Terror Project (APTP) said in a statement following the judge’s decision. “The end of federal oversight does not mean the end of police misconduct. It does not erase the history that brought OPD under federal supervision. And it certainly does not mean Oakland should simply trust OPD to hold itself accountable.”

articles.title: An EV sold every 100 seconds: Australian demand for electric cars more than doubles
articles.excerpt:
A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, ...
articles.body_text:
A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australians are buying electric vehicles at record levels, with sales more than doubling year on year and occurring at a rate equivalent to one EV sold every 100 seconds.

A record 157,957 EV sales occurred between January and June – an 117% increase on the same period last year, according to a new report released by the Electric Vehicle Council.

Comparatively, petrol and diesel vehicle sales decreased by 14% year on year, according to the council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio.

EVs accounted for one in four new vehicles sold in the first half of the year, up 12.1% from the first six months of 2025, the state of EVs report said.

“EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure by households across Australia,” Delvecchio said of the rise, noting that the ongoing fuel crisis was an accelerating factor but was “not the starting gun”.

“It exposed the value of the policy work that had already been done – and made the lower running costs and energy security benefits of EVs much more immediate for Australian households,” she said.

The new figures include about 104,000 battery electric vehicles and 54,000 plug-in hybrids.

As of June, there were 612,000 EVs in the national vehicle fleet. “We are well on track to hit the target of 1 million EVs on Australian roads by next year,” said Aman Gaur, the head of policy and advocacy at the EV Council.

The Australian Capital Territory, where 44% of new cars registered are electric, retained its crown as the nation’s EV capital.

Tarneit, in Melbourne’s west, was the individual postcode with the highest uptake.

A key driver of the growing uptake has been the national vehicle efficiency standard, which requires carmakers to supply new vehicles that meet an average per-kilometre emissions target.

The standard had “substantially increased the options and the price competitiveness of EVs”, with nearly 200 EV models available in 2026, Gaur said.

The council is pushing for the federal government to extend the standard beyond 2029, to align with the government’s 2035 emissions reduction target.

Charging infrastructure had largely kept pace with growing EV demand, the report found, with the number of public charging locations growing to 4,268 across the country.

While Australia was no longer a global laggard compared with other electric car markets, buses and cars were “roaring ahead” of electric trucks and vans, for which sales continued to be less than 1% of their respective markets, Gaur said.

“Every truck that is electric is an upgrade to Australia’s energy security,” Delvecchio said. “We’ve barely touched the sides on that transition.”

The report also found the federal, ACT and NSW governments’ EV policies were “top of the class, while South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Northern Territory have gone backwards”.

“Queensland and the Northern Territory are … moving to back to fossil fuels rather than trying to electrify their transport systems,” Gaur said.

“The most disappointing example of this was when the Queensland government recently invested in 630 diesel buses.

“The diesel buses will be on Queensland roads until the end of the next decade, and they will certainly be polluting the air in Brisbane when the Olympics are held.”

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone's advice to those who are struggling 50 years after 'Rocky' changed his life
articles.excerpt: Actor and filmmaker Sylvester Stallone discusses his unlikely rise to stardom and reflects on the experiences that shaped his career. He also shares some of his biggest filmmaking influences and looks...
articles.body_text:
Actor and filmmaker Sylvester Stallone discusses his unlikely rise to stardom and reflects on the experiences that shaped his career. He also shares some of his biggest filmmaking influences and looks back on the lessons he learned from movies on ‘Special Report.’

Fifty years after "Rocky" made Sylvester Stallone a household name, the 80-year-old says his advice to people who are struggling is "you have nothing to lose" if you try.

"Rocky," a story about a low-level boxer who got the unexpected chance to become a champion, parallels the actor’s own life from being so broke he had to sell his dog to winning the Oscar for the 1976 classic.

"What would you tell the kid who’s sleeping on the bench at Port Authority with $80 in his pocket?" Fox News’ Bret Baier asked Stallone on "Special Report" on Tuesday while discussing his new memoir "The Steps."

'I PLAY ROCKY' REVIVES THE GAMBLE THAT MADE SYLVESTER STALLONE A SUPERSTAR

Sylvester Stallone said his own motto is "I tried." (Getty Images)

"You have nothing to lose. Seriously, you have nothing to lose. With failure you don’t get shot. There’s no firing squad," Stallone said. "The only thing you have to lose is your peace of mind if you don’t try. At least try. You may quit halfway through, but at least say, ‘I tried.’"

Stallone said his own motto is "I tried."

SYLVESTER STALLONE SAYS HE'D BE IN 'BIG TROUBLE' TRYING TO MAKE HIS CAREER IN TODAY'S HOLLYWOOD

As a broke 23-year-old backpacking through the Pyrenees in Europe in 1969, Stallone wrote in the book that a fortune teller predicted he would find fortune by 1976, the same year "Rocky" came out.

"And she said also, ‘A woman will bring you into the circle of attention, and that was my manager Jane Oliver who’s the only one like who plucked me from obscurity," he said.

SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE

Actors Sylvester Stallone and Carl Weathers perform a boxing scene in the 1976 movie "Rocky." (Getty Images)

Early in his career, Stallone went by the name Mike, but decided to go back to Sylvester.

Stallone felt pre-"Rocky" that he was drifting off into "total obscurity" and thought if Humphrey Bogart could make a career with his name, then "Sylvester’s not so bad."

SYLVESTER STALLONE'S 'TULSA KING' SEASON 4 TEASER SPARKS FAN FRENZY: 'THE KING IS BACK!'

Sylvester Stallone as boxer Rocky Balboa trains with a punchbag in the 1976 film "Rocky." (Getty Images)

"I thought, that’s memorable because I’ve never met another Sylvester. So, at least it was just another hook that maybe people would remember as opposed to Mike.

Stallone told Baier that he decided to write his book now because he wanted his children to "understand the journey" it took to get him where he is now.

MATT DAMON SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S 'RUTHLESS' NATURE HAS TAKEN HIM AWAY FROM FATHERHOOD MORE THAN HE'D LIKE

The "Tulsa King" actor called ushering at a theater his "film school," explaining that he would watch three showings a night on his shift and would take notes from films like "M*A*S*H."

"I thought, where do you learn more about a film than in a theater where you actually see a reaction?"

HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER BEHIND 'APOLLO 13' REJECTS POLITICS IN HIS MOVIES, SEEKS TO UNITE AUDIENCES

He said college is "very cloistered," whereas in a theater it’s "instant enjoyment or repulsion or they leave. So, I learned a great, great deal. It’s like with a waiter – you want to learn the restaurant business? Be a waiter."

"I learned more in a movie theater than I would imagine in college," he said.

Stallone, with fellow winner Beatrice Straight, holding his Oscar after winning in 1977. (Getty Images)

TOM CRUISE ADMITS RUMORS ABOUT HIS 'INTENSE' BEHAVIOR ON MOVIE SETS ARE TRUE

Stallone also wrote that the "go the distance" speech in "Rocky" almost didn’t happen because the producers wanted to cut it.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"They did pull the plug," he told Baier. "And I have to say I really did lose my cool at that moment. Very upset. It was the first time I really crossed the line. I said, ‘You have to film this because this is the whole movie philosophy in a nutshell."

JACK NICHOLSON SPOTTED IN RARE PHOTO AS LEGENDARY ACTOR CELEBRATES TURNING 89

Sylvester Stallone said he lost his cool when producers tried to cut the "go the distance" speech in "Rocky." (GC Images)

In the end, the producers gave Stallone one take to get it.

"If the camera shook, if the sound man… I was like ‘Everyone, please be on you A-game.’"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Stallone didn’t believe he was going to win the Academy Award in 1977, and when Jack Nicolson called his name, he said he was shocked and almost "broke down."

The actor dedicated the award to all the people who, like Rocky Balboa, struggle but will always "be there" working hard.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Morocco’s pro-Palestine protests challenge Rabat’s deepening Israel ties
articles.excerpt:
Pro-Palestine protests have spread across several Moroccan cities, with demonstrators demanding an end to diplomatic normalisation with Israel as Rabat deepens ties with Tel Aviv.

The latest mobilisa...
articles.body_text:
Pro-Palestine protests have spread across several Moroccan cities, with demonstrators demanding an end to diplomatic normalisation with Israel as Rabat deepens ties with Tel Aviv.

The latest mobilisation took place on September 27, at the end of three days of action called by the Moroccan Front for Supporting Palestine and Against Normalisation.

They followed a September 16 announcement that Morocco and Israel would elevate their diplomatic missions to full embassies and appoint ambassadors.

On September 25, the Moroccan Committee for Supporting the Nation’s Causes said it had organised 76 events in 45 cities under the slogan “Friday for Al-Aqsa and against normalisation”.

Moroccan media reported gatherings in cities including Rabat, Casablanca, Marrakesh, Tangier, Fez, Agadir, Oujda, Tetouan, Kenitra and Sale. The 76-event figure was the committee’s own count, with no independent national tally of participants.

In Rabat, protesters gathered outside Parliament, while a demonstration in Marrakesh developed into a march through several main streets, according to Lakome. Moroccan media also reported restrictions and arrests in some cities.

The mobilisation faced restrictions in some cities.

In Tangier, local authorities issued a decision banning a planned demonstration on September 27. Achkayen later reported that security forces dispersed hundreds of participants and that more than 12 people were detained, citing its own sources.

Lakome reported that authorities also prevented demonstrations in M’diq, while security forces surrounded a gathering in Agadir to prevent it from becoming a march.

The Moroccan Committee for Supporting the Nation’s Causes subsequently condemned what it described as bans, restrictions and arrests.

The response underscored another dimension of the dispute: Opposition to the relationship with Israel has remained visible on the streets, even as the government has continued to develop official ties.

Morocco restored diplomatic relations with Israel in December 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords framework, alongside Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.

On September 16, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar met in New York at a trilateral summit hosted by US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz.

The three countries confirmed plans to elevate the Moroccan and Israeli diplomatic missions to full embassies and exchange ambassadors.

Morocco and Israel also agreed to conclude agreements on investment protection and avoiding double taxation, expand direct flights and organise high-level reciprocal visits.

The move therefore goes beyond maintaining diplomatic relations established in 2020. It sets out a broader programme of institutional, economic and transport links between the two countries.

For opponents of the relationship, the embassy agreement represents another step in a policy they have rejected since 2020.

Morocco has maintained diplomatic relations with Israel while continuing to publicly support the Palestinian cause and the establishment of a Palestinian state.

For opponents of normalisation, however, the two positions are incompatible, particularly amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

“What has changed is the political context: Normalisation is being consolidated at a time when the war in Gaza has generated unprecedented public anger and intense images of Palestinian suffering,” Kathya K Berrada, senior programmes manager at the Arab Center for Research, told Al Jazeera.

“What we are seeing in Morocco is a growing disconnect between official diplomacy and public sentiment,” Moroccan activist Mouna Rahiani said, citing the latest Arab Opinion Index, which found that 89 percent of Moroccans surveyed opposed their country recognising Israel, while six percent supported it.

“While the state is moving towards deeper and more formal relations with Israel, Moroccans are still taking to the streets to say that Palestine cannot be treated as separate from our political and moral responsibilities,” she said.

The September agreement has brought an existing tension into sharper focus: public mobilisation against normalisation continues while the state pursues closer institutional ties with Israel.

Berrada said there was an important distinction between official policy and popular opinion, arguing that there is not enough reliable public data to establish how many Moroccans support or oppose normalisation.

The timing also matters for Morocco’s Western Sahara policy. The United Nations Security Council is due to consider the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) in October. Its current mandate runs until October 31, 2026.

The September 16 trilateral statement came against the backdrop of US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and Israel’s support for Morocco’s position on the territory.

For Rabat, the relationship with Israel sits within a wider foreign-policy framework in which ties with Washington and international support for its position on Western Sahara remain important.

For opponents of normalisation, however, that strategic calculation does not resolve their objection to closer ties with Israel, particularly while the Palestinian issue remains highly salient.

Ahmed, a Moroccan sociologist who asked to be identified by one name, said the September 16 move was “a continuation of the trilateral agreement of December 10, 2020”, but that Morocco should make the relationship “comprehensive, not selective or partial”.

The protests came days after Morocco held parliamentary elections on September 23.

The final results gave the Authenticity and Modernity Party 97 of the 395 seats, followed by the National Rally of Independents with 66, the Istiqlal Party with 65 and the Party of Justice and Development (PJD) with 54.

The PJD had won 13 seats in 2021. Turnout was 38.08 percent, compared with 50.86 percent in 2021 and 42.27 percent in 2016, according to Morocco’s Ministry of Interior.

It was the PJD in power when Morocco restored relations with Israel in 2020. Then-Prime Minister Saadeddine el-Othmani signed the Morocco-US-Israel joint declaration that December.

The PJD has maintained that opposition to normalisation was a longstanding party position. The party subsequently reaffirmed its rejection of normalisation and relations with Israel, while el-Othmani defended the 2020 decision as a state-level decision.

On September 17, following the announcement of the planned diplomatic upgrade, the PJD’s general secretariat reiterated its opposition to normalisation and to relations and agreements with Israel.

After the election, the PJD’s national council unanimously decided to remain in parliamentary opposition and not participate in the next government.

The PJD’s position has illustrated the limits of using party politics to measure the effect of opposition to normalisation. The party opposed the policy while in government, yet its prime minister signed the 2020 declaration.

Its larger parliamentary presence in 2026 gives the issue a stronger political platform, but does not by itself alter Morocco’s foreign policy.

It has not been established that the Palestine issue or opposition to normalisation was a decisive factor in voting, and neither do the PJD’s gains demonstrate that its position on Israel directly drove its increased representation.

The September demonstrations show that organisations opposed to normalisation retain the ability to mobilise across a wide geographic area. But their effect on government policy is less clear.

“There is an important distinction between state policy and popular opinion. Normalisation is an official state decision, but there is limited reliable public data allowing us to measure the level of popular support for it,” Berrada said.

“It would therefore be difficult to claim that either a majority or a minority of Moroccans endorse the policy.”

That distinction is important when assessing the significance of the protests. Demonstrations can show the strength and persistence of organised opposition, but they do not by themselves establish the views of the wider population or show that government policy will change.

The PJD now has a larger parliamentary presence than it did after the 2021 election, but it remains in opposition. It will be able to voice its opposition to normalisation in Parliament, but will not have a place in government.

At the same time, the September 16 agreement remains part of a broader Moroccan foreign-policy framework involving the United States, Israel and Western Sahara. The Security Council’s consideration of MINURSO in October will provide another diplomatic setting in which Morocco’s position on the territory is under discussion.

For now, the protests demonstrate that opposition to normalisation remains capable of sustained mobilisation, while the government continues to deepen the relationship. Whether that public opposition translates into sustained political pressure remains less clear.

While almost all of these companies offer points and bonus values, Fanatics provides FanCash and betting options. This is a bit subjective — if you’re not interested in Fanatics clothes, memorabilia, etc., you might not like the rewards. However, the FanCash can be used for more bets, which is nice.

Sometimes all you need is to be the only game in town. Hard Rock Bet is the only online sportsbook in Florida, but they still offer a nice welcome bonus of $100 in Bonus Bets when placing a $5 bet.

In our table, we listed a few types of sportsbook promos and offer types. If you’re new to sports betting, you might not be familiar with what they mean, so let’s take a second to explain what the different offer types are.

No-deposit sportsbook bonuses sound appealing because they give new users a promotional credit before they deposit or place a bet with their own money. The catch is that these offers are rare at regulated U.S. sportsbooks, which typically require a qualifying deposit and wager.

When no-deposit offers do appear, they are often tied to a new state launch or a limited sign-up promotion. The bonus is usually small and may come with minimum odds, playthrough and withdrawal requirements, so read the fine print before claiming it. For most bettors, a low-risk bet-and-get offer will provide more practical value.

BetMGM runs one of the most protective welcome offers for bettors who want to start bigger: Up to $1,500 back in bonus bets if the first bet loses. This gives you a chance to make a big splash immediately. If you win, you don’t need the bonus bets. If you lose, you’re still getting a chance to make money back.

How it compares: The $1,500 cap is among the largest safety nets available. Remember the refund is bonus bets, not cash, so real value depends on converting those tokens into wins.

Our Verdict: If you feel very confident in something, and it is your first time betting, this is the spot for you as it provides a bit of a safety net.

One of the nice things about Fanatics is that they offer a few different options to new users. This helps to cater to the wide variety of people interested in picking up sports betting.

How it compares: Instead of just one offer, Fanatics provides a wide variety of offers. You can bet anywhere from $1 to $100 and receive bonuses.

Our Verdict: Fanatics are playing for all bettors, not just the big bettors. There is something for everyone here.

theScore Bet provides a safety-net-style welcome bonus similar to BetMGM, designed for bettors who want protection on a larger opening wager.

How it compares: theScore Bet directly competes with BetMGM's safety-net tier. It caps out slightly lower ($1,000 vs. BetMGM’s $1,500), but splitting the refund into five equal 20% tokens gives you much more flexibility to spread out secondary wagers across different events. Just make sure you use them before they expire.

Our Verdict: The 5-token split makes recovering secondary value noticeably easier than platforms that issue a single massive bonus credit because you don’t need to take a big risk immediately again.

FanDuel is a top-tier option for small-stakes bettors, focusing on high engagement and high-frequency value over single high-risk wagers. Rather than issuing its welcome reward in a single lump sum, FanDuel utilizes a multi-day incentive format that rewards regular participation during your first week on the platform.

How it compares: FanDuel is essentially trying to establish a habit. They get you using the app and making bets five days in a row. Compared to some other sportsbook's guaranteed upfront drop, FanDuel offers a significantly higher potential bonus cap ($250 vs. $200), though it requires consistent daily $5 activity over five days to unlock the maximum reward.

Our Verdict: If you’re going to bet on something every day anyway, but don’t want to bet a lot, this is ideal because you get $250 back.

bet365 frequently changes its welcome offers, and several promotions may appear online at any given time. At the time of review, however, the sportsbook’s website featured one primary offer: Bet $10, Get $200 in bonus bets, win or lose. It is not the biggest promotion in this guide, but the low qualifying wager and guaranteed bonus still make it a worthwhile option for new bettors.

How it compares: bet365 gives you $200 regardless of the outcome of your wager, and they give you those bonus bets immediately, not over time. If you want to bet small ($10) on your first bet, you can bet a bit bigger the next time with the $200 bonus bet.

Our Verdict: This is a nice option for anyone who wants to get started, but give yourself options for a larger wager after the initial bet.

While the welcome offer is a one-time incentive, there are monthly, weekly, and even daily offers from sportsbooks to keep you playing. Profit boosts, same-game parlay insurance, and no-sweat bets are common offers from sportsbooks.

You’re not going to find an NBA promo in August, just as you won’t find an NFL promotion until the season starts. Maybe there will be a promotion you can use in the future or on a future bet, but each book will update options daily for sport-specific promos.

Claiming a sportsbook promo is very easy. It is pretty straightforward and similar at almost every sportsbook app.

For a daily sportsbook bonus, you’re likely going to just place one bet (a parlay or straight bet), and it either hits or not. You have instant gratification (or frustration if your bet loses). With welcome bets, you really need to decide how you want to use bonus bets. The big key is to check expirations so you don’t let them go to waste. Outside of that, you need to know if you have one big bet, or multiple smaller wagers. When you place your initial bet, you might want to plan out how you’ll use the bonus bets over the next few days.

A big headline number does not automatically make a sportsbook promotion a good deal. We look at the offer’s real value compared with the required deposit and qualifying bet, along with the type of promotion and the amount of risk it places on the bettor.

We also consider how clear and fair the terms are, including minimum odds, token restrictions and expiration dates. Ease of claiming, how quickly the bonus is credited, and the strength of ongoing and sport-specific promotions also factor into our rankings. Our ratings are editorially independent, tested when possible and refreshed regularly as sportsbook offers change.

Sports betting should stay fun. If gambling starts to affect your finances, relationships, or wellbeing, these free and confidential resources can help.

The best sportsbook promo depends on your state, budget and betting style. Bettors making a larger first wager may prefer BetMGM’s offer of up to $1,500 back in bonus bets if the first bet loses. If you mainly bet parlays, an ongoing odds boost or same-game parlay promotion may offer more value than a standard welcome offer. There are differing options for each sportsbook that can change from week to week, so it is up to the bettor to decide what is the current best offer.

Bonus bets are promotional credits awarded after you meet a sportsbook’s qualifying requirements. If a $100 bonus bet wins at +100 odds, you receive $100 in winnings, but not the original $100 stake.

A bet-and-get sportsbook promo awards bonus bets after you place a qualifying wager, often whether you win or lose. A first-bet safety net refunds a losing first wager in bonus bets, up to a stated limit, rather than returning the stake as cash.

No-deposit sportsbook bonuses are rare at regulated U.S. sportsbooks, which usually require a deposit and qualifying bet. Some offshore sportsbooks may advertise them, but read the terms carefully because they can include strict playthrough, minimum-odds and withdrawal requirements.

Sportsbook promos are worth it as protection for your bet or as an added incentive for your continued use of their book. It does often require you to use your own money, but the promotions tend to give you better odds than the normal payouts, or give you free bets to make.
